items.title: Frida 17.28.0 Released
items.summary: A Gum release about hooks arriving on time and threads not getting in each other’s way. A hook is now live when attach() returns no matter what other threads are doing, module observers no longer deadlock against hooks, and libraries we looked an export up in can unload again. On macOS and iOS, in-process crash reporters no longer mistake a guarded memory read for a crash. And @BoringApp fixed a crash on startup on iOS 15.0. Interceptor A hook attached on one thread was not live when attach() returned if any other thread was inside an Interceptor transaction at that moment, and every GumJS scope is such a transaction. You would meet this as instrumentation that arrives too late. The typical case is an onAdded handler that hooks a library as it loads, and then misses that library’s first calls. The nesting level of a transaction was global to the Interceptor. It is now per thread: when a thread’s own outermost transaction ends, everything pending is committed, including what other threads have queued inside transactions they still have open. While a commit patches code, hooks are bypassed on the committing thread, so it never waits for a lock that a replacement of, say, thread_suspend() might take. There are a few things a caller can observe differently: A batch can be split. A transaction no longer holds back other threads, so your pending changes may be applied when another thread commits. Hooks can become live earlier than your own end_transaction() , never later. A detach followed by a re-attach inside one transaction may find that the old context was already torn down by another thread’s commit. It then creates a fresh one, which costs an extra patch. flush() no longer waits on other threads. It commits unless the calling thread has a transaction open, so unloading a script completes even while other threads are inside scopes. A thread that exits with a transaction open no longer blocks every later commit in the process. Module observers Process.attachModuleObserver() called onAdded for every loaded module while holding the module registry’s lock. A hook on another thread that needed the registry at that moment deadlocked against it, in two ways. Through the Interceptor, on arm64 since 17.19.0: a hook’s onEnter calls Interceptor.attach() , which looks up the module of its target. And through the JS lock, on any architecture: a hook’s onEnter calls Process.enumerateModules() or Process.findModuleByName() . Once either happened, every other hooked thread and every new thread piled up behind them. The replay no longer runs under the lock. The registry instead tracks that a replay is in progress. A module loaded or unloaded on another thread meanwhile is registered at once, but its notification waits for the replay to end, and is then delivered on the loading thread before the loader returns. So onAdded still completes before the application can call into the library. Enumeration and lookups never wait for a replay, which is what closes both cycles. Unloading Two fixes for libraries that go away. On Linux, FreeBSD and QNX, looking an export up through a Module , or calling ensureInitialized() , took a loader handle and kept it until the module object was disposed. The registry keeps that object until the loader reports the unload, and the handle prevented the unload, so such a library could never unload. ensureInitialized() pinned the same way on Apple systems. The handle is now released after each use, and a module object that outlives its library finds no exports, rather than touching the loader or reading unmapped memory. The registry also decided whether to announce a removal by asking, at unload time, whether the module’s range was cloaked. By then our own allocator could have mapped, and cloaked, new memory over the base the library just left, and the removal was swallowed. This was seen on 32-bit x86 Linux, where the hole a library leaves is the first address reused. The decision is now made when the module is registered. Crash reporters on macOS and iOS On Apple systems a fault is offered to Mach exception ports before it becomes a signal: the thread’s, then the task’s. We catch faults as signals, so the task-level port that every in-process crash reporter installs, be it Crashpad, Sentry, Crashlytics or KSCrash, saw a fault inside one of our guarded scopes first, and treated it as the process crashing. Depending on the reporter, a NativePointer read of a bad address or a memory scan would then hang, or take the process down, rather than throw. Each thread now gets a thread-level port the first time it enters such a scope, which takes precedence over the task’s. Faults inside a scope are caught there, and all others are declined, so they reach the task port and the signal handler as before. Threads that already have a port of their own are left alone. This is done for arm64 and arm64e. Other targets keep to signals. iOS @BoringApp found that Frida exited with SIGBUS during startup on an iPhone 13 running iOS 15.0. Overwriting an executable mapping on that kernel can leave the target inaccessible, which our probe didn’t detect, as it only maps a scratch page. Code is no longer remapped from that kernel on, and the page swap introduced in 17.27.6 is only attempted on macOS, so in-place patching runs everywhere else. Thanks! Enjoy! Changelog interceptor: Make transactions per thread, so a hook is live when attach() returns regardless of other threads. gumjs: Replay modules outside the registry lock, fixing deadlocks between attachModuleObserver() and hooks on other threads. module: Release the loader handle after each use, so libraries can unload. module-registry: Decide cloaking at registration, fixing lost removal notifications. exceptor: Catch faults in guarded scopes before task-level exception ports on macOS and iOS. darwin: Avoid remapping code on iOS 15.0 and newer, and only swap patched pages in on macOS. Thanks @BoringApp !
items.summary_html:
A Gum release about hooks arriving on time and threads not getting in each other’s way. A hook is now live when attach() returns no matter what other threads are doing, module observers no longer deadlock against hooks, and libraries we looked an export up in can unload again. On macOS and iOS, in-process crash reporters no longer mistake a guarded memory read for a crash. And @BoringApp fixed a crash on startup on iOS 15.0.

Interceptor

A hook attached on one thread was not live when attach() returned if any other thread was inside an Interceptor transaction at that moment, and every GumJS scope is such a transaction. You would meet this as instrumentation that arrives too late. The typical case is an onAdded handler that hooks a library as it loads, and then misses that library’s first calls.

The nesting level of a transaction was global to the Interceptor. It is now per thread: when a thread’s own outermost transaction ends, everything pending is committed, including what other threads have queued inside transactions they still have open. While a commit patches code, hooks are bypassed on the committing thread, so it never waits for a lock that a replacement of, say, thread_suspend() might take.

There are a few things a caller can observe differently:

  • A batch can be split. A transaction no longer holds back other threads, so your pending changes may be applied when another thread commits. Hooks can become live earlier than your own end_transaction(), never later.
  • A detach followed by a re-attach inside one transaction may find that the old context was already torn down by another thread’s commit. It then creates a fresh one, which costs an extra patch.
  • flush() no longer waits on other threads. It commits unless the calling thread has a transaction open, so unloading a script completes even while other threads are inside scopes.
  • A thread that exits with a transaction open no longer blocks every later commit in the process.
Module observers

Process.attachModuleObserver() called onAdded for every loaded module while holding the module registry’s lock. A hook on another thread that needed the registry at that moment deadlocked against it, in two ways. Through the Interceptor, on arm64 since 17.19.0: a hook’s onEnter calls Interceptor.attach(), which looks up the module of its target. And through the JS lock, on any architecture: a hook’s onEnter calls Process.enumerateModules() or Process.findModuleByName(). Once either happened, every other hooked thread and every new thread piled up behind them.

The replay no longer runs under the lock. The registry instead tracks that a replay is in progress. A module loaded or unloaded on another thread meanwhile is registered at once, but its notification waits for the replay to end, and is then delivered on the loading thread before the loader returns. So onAdded still completes before the application can call into the library. Enumeration and lookups never wait for a replay, which is what closes both cycles.

Unloading

Two fixes for libraries that go away. On Linux, FreeBSD and QNX, looking an export up through a Module, or calling ensureInitialized(), took a loader handle and kept it until the module object was disposed. The registry keeps that object until the loader reports the unload, and the handle prevented the unload, so such a library could never unload. ensureInitialized() pinned the same way on Apple systems. The handle is now released after each use, and a module object that outlives its library finds no exports, rather than touching the loader or reading unmapped memory.

The registry also decided whether to announce a removal by asking, at unload time, whether the module’s range was cloaked. By then our own allocator could have mapped, and cloaked, new memory over the base the library just left, and the removal was swallowed. This was seen on 32-bit x86 Linux, where the hole a library leaves is the first address reused. The decision is now made when the module is registered.

Crash reporters on macOS and iOS

On Apple systems a fault is offered to Mach exception ports before it becomes a signal: the thread’s, then the task’s. We catch faults as signals, so the task-level port that every in-process crash reporter installs, be it Crashpad, Sentry, Crashlytics or KSCrash, saw a fault inside one of our guarded scopes first, and treated it as the process crashing. Depending on the reporter, a NativePointer read of a bad address or a memory scan would then hang, or take the process down, rather than throw.

Each thread now gets a thread-level port the first time it enters such a scope, which takes precedence over the task’s. Faults inside a scope are caught there, and all others are declined, so they reach the task port and the signal handler as before. Threads that already have a port of their own are left alone. This is done for arm64 and arm64e. Other targets keep to signals.

iOS

@BoringApp found that Frida exited with SIGBUS during startup on an iPhone 13 running iOS 15.0. Overwriting an executable mapping on that kernel can leave the target inaccessible, which our probe didn’t detect, as it only maps a scratch page. Code is no longer remapped from that kernel on, and the page swap introduced in 17.27.6 is only attempted on macOS, so in-place patching runs everywhere else. Thanks!

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • interceptor: Make transactions per thread, so a hook is live when attach() returns regardless of other threads.
  • gumjs: Replay modules outside the registry lock, fixing deadlocks between attachModuleObserver() and hooks on other threads.
  • module: Release the loader handle after each use, so libraries can unload.
  • module-registry: Decide cloaking at registration, fixing lost removal notifications.
  • exceptor: Catch faults in guarded scopes before task-level exception ports on macOS and iOS.
  • darwin: Avoid remapping code on iOS 15.0 and newer, and only swap patched pages in on macOS. Thanks @BoringApp!

items.title: Moving Beyond Static Cookie Banners: Implementing Zero-Leakage Real-Time Consent Management
items.summary: A cookie banner is a user interface requirement, not a control. Many sites display a cookie consent banner giving you options to opt-in or opt-out while the tag manager has already loaded analytics, advertising pixels and session replay, so personal data reaches third parties before the visitor makes any choice and this has caused pre-settlement demand letters for California Invasion of Privacy Act claims. Real-time consent management closes that gap by tying the recorded consent state to what the browser is actually allowed to execute. For privacy officers and security leaders this is familiar ground. Third-party JavaScript is an unmanaged supply chain in your customers’ browsers, and the tags that leak data before consent choices run on the same infrastructure attackers have used to hide card skimmers inside Google Tag Manager containers . This guide covers the architecture, standards, evidence and metrics a CISO needs. This article is informational and is not legal advice; consult privacy counsel on how these laws apply to your organization. Why static banners give a false sense of security Most consent failures come from execution order, not banner wording. The consent script and the tag manager load in parallel, and tags set to fire on page view run before any consent state exists. The banner then records a “reject” that nothing downstream enforces. Three patterns recur in audits: pre-consent firing, where non-essential vendors receive requests on first load; post-reject leakage, where cookies persist or scripts keep sending events after a refusal; and signal blindness, where the site ignores browser opt-outs such as Global Privacy Control (GPC). None of these show in the banner itself, only in the network log. That is why real-time consent management treats consent as a runtime control with telemetry, not a page element legal approves once a year. What regulators have actually penalized The most recent actions show where enforcement is heading. In the past 60 days, California regulators have announced five CCPA penalties. Four of them target the same thing: cookies, pixels and trackers that keep firing after a consumer opts out. On 10 November 2026, CalPrivacy fined FedEx $2.975 million . The agency alleged that tracking on fedex.com sent device and user identifiers to advertising companies while the privacy policy said FedEx did not sell or share personal information. It also alleged that the site had no “Do Not Sell or Share” link, ignored GPC, and kept sharing some visitors’ data after they switched tracking off in the cookie panel. Jenner & Block’s analysis covers the order’s three-year testing obligations. On 17 November 2026, CalPrivacy fined Hertz $1.55 million . The agency alleged that Hertz kept sharing identifiers and rental-search details with ad-tech companies despite GPC signals. On Dollar.com and Thrifty.com, the “Manage Cookies” window showed every toggle as off, but closing it with the X instead of clicking “Save Changes” switched advertising cookies back on. Under the order, Hertz must check for GPC before trackers load, test opt-outs every quarter, and review its consent management platform independently rather than relying on its vendor’s word. The same day, the agency fined C.C. Filson Co. $217,987 for ignoring GPC in both browser-based and server-side sharing with ad-tech companies. That fine was reportedly reduced because Filson showed it could not pay more. On 19 November 2026, CalPrivacy fined Polaris $910,986 in a joint action with the Minnesota Attorney General , who added $150,000 under Minnesota’s privacy law. The agency alleged that clicking “Decline All” in Polaris’s privacy pop-up did not stop all sharing, and that in one instance the click itself fired a Meta pixel. The Attorney General is active too. In late October 2026, the AG settled with Lyft for $1.8 million over app-based ad sharing with no in-app opt-out. To opt out, users had to log in again on a separate webpage and hand over more personal information. These cases build on earlier precedent. The California Attorney General’s first public CCPA settlement, announced on 24 August 2022 , required Sephora to pay $1.2 million. The AG alleged that Sephora failed to process opt-outs sent through user-enabled global privacy controls, and required it to honor GPC going forward. According to Crowell & Moring’s analysis , the complaint also alleged that third-party cookies, pixels and SDKs sent browsing and purchase data to advertising and analytics companies. In July 2025, the AG announced a $1.55 million settlement with Healthline Media whether the court has since approved the Healthline settlement]. Hunton reports allegations that the banner did not disable advertising cookies after an opt-out, and that article titles suggesting a diagnosis were shared for targeting. The California Privacy Protection Agency’s first enforcement decision, announced on 12 March 2025 , fined American Honda $632,500. Among other findings, Covington notes that opting out of cross-context behavioral advertising in Honda’s cookie management tool took more steps than opting back in, which conflicts with the regulations’ symmetry requirement. In Europe, France’s CNIL fined Google €100 million and Amazon €35 million in December 2020 for placing advertising cookies without prior consent or adequate information . In September 2025 it fined two Google entities a combined €325 million , finding in part that refusing personalized advertising cookies during Gmail account creation was harder than accepting them. The EDPB Cookie Banner Taskforce report of 18 January 2023 sets what it calls a minimum threshold. Most authorities expect a reject option on the first layer. The report treats pre-ticked boxes, reject options offered only as a link, contrast that steers users to “accept all,” and legitimate interest claims for non-essential cookies as problems. The US pressure is also multi-state. On 9 September 2025, the attorneys general of California, Colorado and Connecticut, with the CPPA, announced a joint sweep of businesses that ignore GPC. The Polaris action shows that this cooperation now produces joint penalties. The common thread is that regulators test what the browser does, not what the banner says. Hertz’s toggles looked off and Polaris’s “Decline All” looked like a refusal, but the trackers kept firing. Blocking by default: the core of real-time consent management Nothing non-essential executes until a valid consent state exists for its category, checked at the moment of execution rather than once at page load. That requires control at two layers: the HTML that ships with the page, and the tag manager that injects scripts later. Script type rewriting Browsers do not execute a script element whose type is not a JavaScript MIME type. Shipping third-party tags as type=”text/plain” with a data-category attribute keeps the markup inert until consent code rebuilds the element. The pattern below is illustrative and framework-neutral; note that it releases scripts only after the consent record is saved. data-src=”https://analytics.example.com/tag.js”> Changing the type attribute on an existing node does not trigger execution, so the element has to be rebuilt, and iframes and pixels need the same treatment through data-src. Scripts injected by other scripts need a MutationObserver or a consent platform’s DOM interception layer, because inert markup only protects what you ship directly. Tag manager consent gating Most enterprise tracking runs through a tag manager, so HTML rewriting is not enough on its own. In Google Tag Manager, every non-Google tag should carry an explicit consent requirement and fire on a consent-update event pushed by the consent platform, never on the generic page-view trigger. Treat container publish rights as privileged access, since the concealed JavaScript in recent Magecart campaigns relied on the same trust that marketing tags enjoy. Some of those injected scripts even showed fake payment errors at checkout to harvest card details twice. A Content Security Policy allowlist of approved script origins, run in report-only mode first, adds an independent alert when a script outside the approved inventory appears. Consent Mode v2, TCF v2.2 and GPC: getting the signals right Google Consent Mode v2: basic versus advanced Google’s consent mode documentation describes two implementations. In basic mode, Google tags do not load until the user interacts with the banner, and if the user declines, nothing is sent, not even the consent status. In advanced mode, tags load immediately with consent defaulted to denied and send cookieless pings, which supports advertiser-specific conversion modeling. Version 2 added ad_user_data and ad_personalization to the existing storage types. The default-denied command must run before any Google tag loads, as in the illustrative snippet below [VERIFY: parameter names and wait_for_update behavior against Google’s current “Set up consent mode on websites” guide, which could not be retrieved during research]. Choosing a mode is a risk decision, not a marketing default. Google says advanced-mode pings can include a timestamp, user agent and referrer, sent before any choice, so counsel should approve it per jurisdiction. Basic mode is the closer match to zero leakage, at the cost of weaker modeling. IAB TCF v2.2 The IAB Europe Transparency and Consent Framework passes consent to ad tech vendors as a TC string. Version 2.2 launched on 16 May 2023 with a 30 September 2023 implementation deadline, and according to IAB UK it removed legitimate interest as a basis for advertising and content personalization purposes 3 to 6, required the vendor count on the first layer and required easy withdrawal. A TC string only protects users if vendor scripts stay blocked until it says yes. Global Privacy Control and the US state laws Under the CCPA regulations (section 7025), a business must treat an opt-out preference signal such as GPC as a valid request to opt out of sale or sharing. Revised rules effective 1 January 2026 also require the business to display whether it processed the signal, according to Nelson Mullins , with “Opt-Out Request Preference Signal Honored” given as an example. California is not alone. Wilson Sonsini lists Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Oregon, Montana, Texas, New Jersey, Minnesota and New Hampshire as also requiring businesses to honor universal opt-out signals, some with later effective dates. GPC arrives as the Sec-GPC: 1 request header and as navigator.globalPrivacyControl in JavaScript, and it should drive a server-side suppression decision as well as a client-side block. // Illustrative: map GPC to an opt-out before any sale/share tag can fire if (navigator.globalPrivacyControl === true && geo.appliesUSOptOut) { cmp.saveConsent({ marketing: false, saleShare: false, source: ‘gpc’ }); cmp.showStatus(‘Opt-Out Request Preference Signal Honored’); } Browser signals have limits. Researchers reported that Meta and Yandex used localhost connections on Android to link web browsing to app identities , so client-side controls must be backed by contracts and server-side suppression. Proof of consent and drift monitoring Consent records that hold up GDPR Article 7(1) puts the burden on the controller, which “shall be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented.” Article 7(3) adds that withdrawing must be as easy as giving consent. A consent log therefore needs enough context to reconstruct what the user saw and what the site did next. An illustrative record: { “record_id”: “c7f3e2a1-5b0d-4c1e-9a77-2f18d0b4e6aa”, “subject_id”: “pseudo-8d41f0”, “captured_at”: “2026-11-17T09:41:07.312Z”, “jurisdiction”: “EU-FR”, “banner_version”: “2026.11-r3”, “ui_text_sha256”: “4be1c9…”, “action”: “reject_all_first_layer”, “categories”: { “necessary”: true, “analytics”: false, “marketing”: false }, “signals”: { “gpc”: false, “tcf_string_present”: true }, “scripts_released”: [], “page_url”: “https://www.example.com/pricing” } Store records append-only, keyed to a pseudonymous ID, with a retention period counsel approves. The banner version and text hash show which wording was live that day, and scripts_released links consent telemetry to actual quarantine. Drift monitoring Consent configurations decay as marketing adds pixels, vendors change domains and plugins inject tags outside the tag manager. Automated tests that load key pages in a clean browser and assert on the network log catch this before a regulator does. // drift-check.spec.js (illustrative Playwright test) const { test, expect } = require(‘@playwright/test’); const NON_ESSENTIAL = [/doubleclick\.net/, /facebook\.com\/tr/, /hotjar\.com/, /tiktok\.com/]; for (const mode of [‘no-interaction’, ‘reject-all’, ‘gpc’]) { test(‘no non-essential requests: ‘ + mode, async ({ browser }) => { const context = await browser.newContext( mode === ‘gpc’ ? { extraHTTPHeaders: { ‘Sec-GPC’: ‘1’ } } : {} ); if (mode === ‘gpc’) { await context.addInitScript(() => { Object.defineProperty(navigator, ‘globalPrivacyControl’, { get: () => true }); }); } const page = await context.newPage(); const hits = []; page.on(‘request’, r => { if (NON_ESSENTIAL.some(p => p.test(r.url()))) hits.push(r.url()); }); await page.goto(‘https://staging.example.com/’, { waitUntil: ‘networkidle’ }); if (mode === ‘reject-all’) { await page.getByRole(‘button’, { name: /reject all/i }).click(); await page.reload({ waitUntil: ‘networkidle’ }); } expect(hits).toEqual([]); await context.close(); }); } Run it on every container publish and on a schedule. Skimming campaigns that reuse code across lookalike analytics domains show why an unknown domain in this log is a security finding as well as a privacy one. Governance metrics and a rollout plan for CISOs Report consent alongside other control effectiveness metrics. The table is an illustrative starting set; agree targets with legal and marketing. Metric How to measure Illustrative target Owner Pre-consent non-essential requests Synthetic crawl of top templates with no interaction 0 AppSec Post-reject leakage Requests or cookies from blocked categories after reject 0 Privacy engineering GPC honor rate Share of GPC test sessions with sale/share tags suppressed and status shown 100% Privacy engineering Unclassified scripts New script origins without a category Classified within 5 business days GRC Consent record completeness Sampled records with timestamp, banner version, text hash and action 100% Privacy / Legal Drift time to remediate Detection to fix for consent test failures Under 72 hours Web platform Choice parity Banner variants with first-layer reject and equal styling 100% in EU/UK Legal / UX Consented measurement coverage Opt-in rate and modeled conversion share Trend only Marketing analytics Mapping to the NIST Privacy Framework The NIST Privacy Framework groups privacy outcomes into five functions: Identify-P, Govern-P, Control-P, Communicate-P and Protect-P. Tracker inventory maps to Identify-P and banner policy and vendor contracts to Govern-P. Script blocking and opt-out handling are Control-P outcomes, banner text and the GPC notice are Communicate-P, and securing consent logs and tag manager access is Protect-P. Implementation rollout plan The timeline below is illustrative. Weeks 1-2, discovery: crawl top templates in all consent states, export every tag manager container, and inventory vendors with purpose and contract status. Weeks 3-4, classify and decide: categorize every script, get legal sign-off on jurisdiction rules, and choose a Consent Mode variant per region. Weeks 5-6, block by default in staging: convert hard-coded tags to text/plain, add consent requirements to all tag manager tags, and fix what breaks. Weeks 7-8, signals: ship Consent Mode defaults, TCF v2.2 where ad tech requires it, and GPC handling with the status notice and server-side suppression. Weeks 9-10, evidence: deploy append-only consent records, retention rules and an export path for inquiries. Week 11 onward, monitor and govern: run drift tests in CI and on a schedule, and report the KPI table monthly. Do not skip staging. Blocking by default will break dashboards, A/B testing tools and chat widgets, and teams need time to rebuild the ones that are actually essential. How Captain Compliance approaches this Captain Compliance is one of several vendors here and now ranks number 1 in our rankings that include Ketch, OneTrust, Osano, Transcend Privacy, and TrustArc the legacy providers. According to the privacy software reports, its consent management solution provides a customizable banner deployable through Google Tag Manager, a JavaScript snippet, or Shopify and WordPress integrations, and the company protects and documents universal orchestration consent “across web, mobile, CRMs, and CTV. Captain Compliance platform intercepts non-essential scripts at the DOM level before transmission rather than only logging consent, and produces timestamped technical receipts intended for responding to demand letters and regulators. The company says it deploys as a single lightweight tag and combines scanning, consent, vendor data mapping and consumer rights in one platform. The Captain pixel and Cookie Scanner called “patrol”, runs six phases in fresh browsers (pre-consent, accept, reject, GPC, settings panel and IAB TCF v2), flags manipulative banner design and scores results per jurisdiction. A separate product from the traditional cookie scanner for classification, Patrol, is described as flagging drift from an approved state. Competitors to this product are ObservePoint, Privado AI, Tag Inspector, Guidewire Cyence, VaultJS, and Privaini. Patrol by Captain Compliance is the newest tool to hit the market. “Compliance and privacy is not an administrative checkbox or an aesthetic banner—it is a technical control. If your systems cannot prove when, where, and how user data was isolated or fulfilled at the exact millisecond of interaction, you are operating with an open legal flank and thankfully Captain Compliance has become the company to protect businesses globally from privacy violations and litigation threats,” said Richart Ruddie, CEO, Captain Compliance during a recent television interview. Whichever cookie consent manager you shortlist, run a proof of concept on a staging copy of a high-traffic page. Users who have tested usercentrics cookiebot, cookieYes, and termly found that the lower end of the market comes with huge integration challenges and oftentimes the tools do not work. In the higher end of the market where MineOS, BigID, OneTrust, Ketch, and Captain Compliance plays has been said by Accenture analysts that you can’t compare the lower end of the market to the higher end tools and Captain along with a few others have found a way to play nice on both ends. Confirm with your own Playwright or DevTools capture that no non-essential requests fire before a choice or after reject, that GPC suppresses sale and sharing tags, and that Consent Mode defaults load before any Google tag. Then ask for the consent record of a specific test session and check it against the fields above. To run that test plan against a live deployment, See the World’s Best Cookie Consent Manager in Action which is our new number 1 ranked consent management platform and see why when you test pre-consent, reject and Global Privacy Control signals.

The agency alleged that clicking “Decline All” in Polaris’s privacy pop-up did not stop all sharing, and that in one instance the click itself fired a Meta pixel.

The Attorney General is active too. In late October 2026, the AG settled with Lyft for $1.8 million over app-based ad sharing with no in-app opt-out. To opt out, users had to log in again on a separate webpage and hand over more personal information.

These cases build on earlier precedent. The California Attorney General’s first public CCPA settlement, announced on 24 August 2022, required Sephora to pay $1.2 million.

The AG alleged that Sephora failed to process opt-outs sent through user-enabled global privacy controls, and required it to honor GPC going forward.

According to Crowell & Moring’s analysis, the complaint also alleged that third-party cookies, pixels and SDKs sent browsing and purchase data to advertising and analytics companies.

In July 2025, the AG announced a $1.55 million settlement with Healthline Media whether the court has since approved the Healthline settlement].

Hunton reports allegations that the banner did not disable advertising cookies after an opt-out, and that article titles suggesting a diagnosis were shared for targeting.

The California Privacy Protection Agency’s first enforcement decision, announced on 12 March 2025, fined American Honda $632,500.

Among other findings, Covington notes that opting out of cross-context behavioral advertising in Honda’s cookie management tool took more steps than opting back in, which conflicts with the regulations’ symmetry requirement.

In Europe, France’s CNIL fined Google €100 million and Amazon €35 million in December 2020 for placing advertising cookies without prior consent or adequate information.

In September 2025 it fined two Google entities a combined €325 million, finding in part that refusing personalized advertising cookies during Gmail account creation was harder than accepting them.

The EDPB Cookie Banner Taskforce report of 18 January 2023 sets what it calls a minimum threshold. Most authorities expect a reject option on the first layer.

The report treats pre-ticked boxes, reject options offered only as a link, contrast that steers users to “accept all,” and legitimate interest claims for non-essential cookies as problems.

The US pressure is also multi-state. On 9 September 2025, the attorneys general of California, Colorado and Connecticut, with the CPPA, announced a joint sweep of businesses that ignore GPC.

The Polaris action shows that this cooperation now produces joint penalties. The common thread is that regulators test what the browser does, not what the banner says. Hertz’s toggles looked off and Polaris’s “Decline All” looked like a refusal, but the trackers kept firing.

Blocking by default: the core of real-time consent management

Nothing non-essential executes until a valid consent state exists for its category, checked at the moment of execution rather than once at page load.

That requires control at two layers: the HTML that ships with the page, and the tag manager that injects scripts later.

Script type rewriting

Browsers do not execute a script element whose type is not a JavaScript MIME type. Shipping third-party tags as type=”text/plain” with a data-category attribute keeps the markup inert until consent code rebuilds the element. 

The pattern below is illustrative and framework-neutral; note that it releases scripts only after the consent record is saved.


        data-src=”https://analytics.example.com/tag.js”>




Changing the type attribute on an existing node does not trigger execution, so the element has to be rebuilt, and iframes and pixels need the same treatment through data-src. 

Scripts injected by other scripts need a MutationObserver or a consent platform’s DOM interception layer, because inert markup only protects what you ship directly.

Tag manager consent gating

Most enterprise tracking runs through a tag manager, so HTML rewriting is not enough on its own. In Google Tag Manager, every non-Google tag should carry an explicit consent requirement and fire on a consent-update event pushed by the consent platform, never on the generic page-view trigger. 

Treat container publish rights as privileged access, since the concealed JavaScript in recent Magecart campaigns relied on the same trust that marketing tags enjoy.

Some of those injected scripts even showed fake payment errors at checkout to harvest card details twice.

A Content Security Policy allowlist of approved script origins, run in report-only mode first, adds an independent alert when a script outside the approved inventory appears.

Consent Mode v2, TCF v2.2 and GPC: getting the signals right Google Consent Mode v2: basic versus advanced

Google’s consent mode documentation describes two implementations. In basic mode, Google tags do not load until the user interacts with the banner, and if the user declines, nothing is sent, not even the consent status. 

In advanced mode, tags load immediately with consent defaulted to denied and send cookieless pings, which supports advertiser-specific conversion modeling.

Version 2 added ad_user_data and ad_personalization to the existing storage types. The default-denied command must run before any Google tag loads, as in the illustrative snippet below [VERIFY: parameter names and wait_for_update behavior against Google’s current “Set up consent mode on websites” guide, which could not be retrieved during research].






Choosing a mode is a risk decision, not a marketing default. Google says advanced-mode pings can include a timestamp, user agent and referrer, sent before any choice, so counsel should approve it per jurisdiction.

Basic mode is the closer match to zero leakage, at the cost of weaker modeling.

IAB TCF v2.2

The IAB Europe Transparency and Consent Framework passes consent to ad tech vendors as a TC string.

Version 2.2 launched on 16 May 2023 with a 30 September 2023 implementation deadline, and according to IAB UK it removed legitimate interest as a basis for advertising and content personalization purposes 3 to 6, required the vendor count on the first layer and required easy withdrawal.

A TC string only protects users if vendor scripts stay blocked until it says yes.

Global Privacy Control and the US state laws

Under the CCPA regulations (section 7025), a business must treat an opt-out preference signal such as GPC as a valid request to opt out of sale or sharing.

Revised rules effective 1 January 2026 also require the business to display whether it processed the signal, according to Nelson Mullins, with “Opt-Out Request Preference Signal Honored” given as an example.

California is not alone. Wilson Sonsini lists Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Oregon, Montana, Texas, New Jersey, Minnesota and New Hampshire as also requiring businesses to honor universal opt-out signals, some with later effective dates. 

GPC arrives as the Sec-GPC: 1 request header and as navigator.globalPrivacyControl in JavaScript, and it should drive a server-side suppression decision as well as a client-side block.

// Illustrative: map GPC to an opt-out before any sale/share tag can fire
if (navigator.globalPrivacyControl === true && geo.appliesUSOptOut) {
  cmp.saveConsent({ marketing: false, saleShare: false, source: ‘gpc’ });
  cmp.showStatus(‘Opt-Out Request Preference Signal Honored’);
}

Browser signals have limits. Researchers reported that Meta and Yandex used localhost connections on Android to link web browsing to app identities, so client-side controls must be backed by contracts and server-side suppression.

Proof of consent and drift monitoring Consent records that hold up

GDPR Article 7(1) puts the burden on the controller, which “shall be able to demonstrate that the data subject has consented.” Article 7(3) adds that withdrawing must be as easy as giving consent.

A consent log therefore needs enough context to reconstruct what the user saw and what the site did next. An illustrative record:

{
  “record_id”: “c7f3e2a1-5b0d-4c1e-9a77-2f18d0b4e6aa”,
  “subject_id”: “pseudo-8d41f0”,
  “captured_at”: “2026-11-17T09:41:07.312Z”,
  “jurisdiction”: “EU-FR”,
  “banner_version”: “2026.11-r3”,
  “ui_text_sha256”: “4be1c9…”,
  “action”: “reject_all_first_layer”,
  “categories”: { “necessary”: true, “analytics”: false, “marketing”: false },
  “signals”: { “gpc”: false, “tcf_string_present”: true },
  “scripts_released”: [],
  “page_url”: “https://www.example.com/pricing”
}

Store records append-only, keyed to a pseudonymous ID, with a retention period counsel approves. The banner version and text hash show which wording was live that day, and scripts_released links consent telemetry to actual quarantine.

Drift monitoring

Consent configurations decay as marketing adds pixels, vendors change domains and plugins inject tags outside the tag manager. Automated tests that load key pages in a clean browser and assert on the network log catch this before a regulator does.

// drift-check.spec.js (illustrative Playwright test)
const { test, expect } = require(‘@playwright/test’);
const NON_ESSENTIAL = [/doubleclick\.net/, /facebook\.com\/tr/, /hotjar\.com/, /tiktok\.com/];

for (const mode of [‘no-interaction’, ‘reject-all’, ‘gpc’]) {
  test(‘no non-essential requests: ‘ + mode, async ({ browser }) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext(
      mode === ‘gpc’ ? { extraHTTPHeaders: { ‘Sec-GPC’: ‘1’ } } : {}
    );
    if (mode === ‘gpc’) {
      await context.addInitScript(() => {
        Object.defineProperty(navigator, ‘globalPrivacyControl’, { get: () => true });
      });
    }
    const page = await context.newPage();
    const hits = [];
    page.on(‘request’, r => {
      if (NON_ESSENTIAL.some(p => p.test(r.url()))) hits.push(r.url());
    });
    await page.goto(‘https://staging.example.com/’, { waitUntil: ‘networkidle’ });
    if (mode === ‘reject-all’) {
      await page.getByRole(‘button’, { name: /reject all/i }).click();
      await page.reload({ waitUntil: ‘networkidle’ });
    }
    expect(hits).toEqual([]);
    await context.close();
  });
}

Run it on every container publish and on a schedule. Skimming campaigns that reuse code across lookalike analytics domains show why an unknown domain in this log is a security finding as well as a privacy one.

Governance metrics and a rollout plan for CISOs

Report consent alongside other control effectiveness metrics. The table is an illustrative starting set; agree targets with legal and marketing.

MetricHow to measureIllustrative targetOwnerPre-consent non-essential requestsSynthetic crawl of top templates with no interaction0AppSecPost-reject leakageRequests or cookies from blocked categories after reject0Privacy engineeringGPC honor rateShare of GPC test sessions with sale/share tags suppressed and status shown100%Privacy engineeringUnclassified scriptsNew script origins without a categoryClassified within 5 business daysGRCConsent record completenessSampled records with timestamp, banner version, text hash and action100%Privacy / LegalDrift time to remediateDetection to fix for consent test failuresUnder 72 hoursWeb platformChoice parityBanner variants with first-layer reject and equal styling100% in EU/UKLegal / UXConsented measurement coverageOpt-in rate and modeled conversion shareTrend onlyMarketing analytics Mapping to the NIST Privacy Framework

The NIST Privacy Framework groups privacy outcomes into five functions: Identify-P, Govern-P, Control-P, Communicate-P and Protect-P.

Tracker inventory maps to Identify-P and banner policy and vendor contracts to Govern-P. Script blocking and opt-out handling are Control-P outcomes, banner text and the GPC notice are Communicate-P, and securing consent logs and tag manager access is Protect-P.

Implementation rollout plan

The timeline below is illustrative.

  1. Weeks 1-2, discovery: crawl top templates in all consent states, export every tag manager container, and inventory vendors with purpose and contract status.
  2. Weeks 3-4, classify and decide: categorize every script, get legal sign-off on jurisdiction rules, and choose a Consent Mode variant per region.
  3. Weeks 5-6, block by default in staging: convert hard-coded tags to text/plain, add consent requirements to all tag manager tags, and fix what breaks.
  4. Weeks 7-8, signals: ship Consent Mode defaults, TCF v2.2 where ad tech requires it, and GPC handling with the status notice and server-side suppression.
  5. Weeks 9-10, evidence: deploy append-only consent records, retention rules and an export path for inquiries.
  6. Week 11 onward, monitor and govern: run drift tests in CI and on a schedule, and report the KPI table monthly.

Do not skip staging. Blocking by default will break dashboards, A/B testing tools and chat widgets, and teams need time to rebuild the ones that are actually essential.

How Captain Compliance approaches this

Captain Compliance is one of several vendors here and now ranks number 1 in our rankings that include Ketch, OneTrust, Osano, Transcend Privacy,  and TrustArc the legacy providers.

According to the privacy software reports, its consent management solution provides a customizable banner deployable through Google Tag Manager, a JavaScript snippet, or Shopify and WordPress integrations, and the company protects and documents universal orchestration consent “across web, mobile, CRMs, and CTV.

Captain Compliance platform intercepts non-essential scripts at the DOM level before transmission rather than only logging consent, and produces timestamped technical receipts intended for responding to demand letters and regulators.

The company says it deploys as a single lightweight tag and combines scanning, consent, vendor data mapping and consumer rights in one platform.

The Captain pixel and Cookie Scanner called “patrol”, runs six phases in fresh browsers (pre-consent, accept, reject, GPC, settings panel and IAB TCF v2), flags manipulative banner design and scores results per jurisdiction.

A separate product from the traditional cookie scanner for classification, Patrol, is described as flagging drift from an approved state. Competitors to this product are ObservePoint, Privado AI, Tag Inspector, Guidewire Cyence, VaultJS, and Privaini.

Patrol by Captain Compliance is the newest tool to hit the market. 

“Compliance and privacy is not an administrative checkbox or an aesthetic banner—it is a technical control. If your systems cannot prove when, where, and how user data was isolated or fulfilled at the exact millisecond of interaction, you are operating with an open legal flank and thankfully Captain Compliance has become the company to protect businesses globally from privacy violations and litigation threats,” said Richart Ruddie, CEO, Captain Compliance during a recent television interview.

Whichever cookie consent manager you shortlist, run a proof of concept on a staging copy of a high-traffic page.

Users who have tested usercentrics cookiebot, cookieYes, and termly found that the lower end of the market comes with huge integration challenges and oftentimes the tools do not work.

In the higher end of the market where MineOS, BigID, OneTrust, Ketch, and Captain Compliance plays has been said by Accenture analysts that you can’t compare the lower end of the market to the higher end tools and Captain along with a few others have found a way to play nice on both ends.   

Confirm with your own Playwright or DevTools capture that no non-essential requests fire before a choice or after reject, that GPC suppresses sale and sharing tags, and that Consent Mode defaults load before any Google tag.

Then ask for the consent record of a specific test session and check it against the fields above.

To run that test plan against a live deployment, See the World’s Best Cookie Consent Manager in Action which is our new number 1 ranked consent management platform and see why when you test pre-consent, reject and Global Privacy Control signals.

items.title: Hackers Hide Password-Stealing Malware in GitHub Code, Putting Software Downloads at Risk
items.summary: Hackers slipped password-stealing malware into open GitHub pull requests at AsyncAPI Generator, CircuitVerse and Open Food Facts. At CircuitVerse, the code ran in the automated release workflow that built desktop software for Windows, Linux and macOS. Maintainers removed 40 installers from GitHub Actions on November 25, 2026, more than a month after the files became available to download. The malicious changes arrived on October 19 in pull requests from the GitHub account Eternity0207 . GitHub later suspended the account and removed its 217 pull requests. A review found no loader in the 145 requests that had been merged. That distinction matters: an automated build can run code from a proposed change before maintainers approve or merge it. Researchers at StepSecurity identified the code as PolinRider after decoding samples from all three projects. Earlier reporting on hidden PolinRider JavaScript loaders documented the same family disguising code as fonts and hiding it in build files. Victims who examined infected machines reported that later stages targeted browser passwords, macOS Keychain data and GitHub credentials. The report did not establish that any of the three projects lost secrets. Hackers Hide Password-Stealing Malware in GitHub Code The attackers used force-pushes, which replace the commit history on a branch, to insert malicious changes into pull requests that were already open. At AsyncAPI, the unsigned commits reused the dates and messages of legitimate signed commits. They remained visible for roughly 30 to 40 minutes before another update replaced them. A reviewer looking only at the final set of changes would not have seen the malware. The loader appeared in JavaScript files used by build and test tools. Some copies sat beyond hundreds of tabs, making an added line look blank in GitHub’s code review view. CircuitVerse also received a fake font tied to a Visual Studio Code task. As earlier coverage of malware targeting code editors shows, opening an unreviewed project can be enough to run code when automatic workspace tasks are enabled. The three projects saw different outcomes. AsyncAPI required approval for workflows from outside contributors, so neither of its two affected pull requests ran in continuous integration (CI), the system that automatically builds and tests changes. Malicious Files for GitHub (Source – StepSecurity) Open Food Facts ran builds on four affected commits; all four failed, and maintainers rotated a secret. CircuitVerse ran the loader and published installers as workflow artifacts, meaning users could download them from the build pages. That exposure differs from the earlier AsyncAPI npm package compromise , which reached users through the project’s package registry. Here, the affected CircuitVerse files came from pull-request builds. StepSecurity did not report how many users downloaded or ran them. Anyone who ran one should treat the device as potentially compromised and replace the installer with a clean release from a trusted source. How to Check for PolinRider Exposure StepSecurity found the loader in 576 of 622 repositories it checked, across 311 GitHub accounts. That is a count of confirmed findings in the sample, not a platform-wide estimate. Like earlier PolinRider infections in npm , the loader used Ethereum data to locate its next-stage server. Blocking one IP address therefore would not cover the campaign as the server changed. Maintainers should review October workflow logs, pull-request timelines and build outputs, even if the final code looks clean. Require approval for workflows from all external contributors, require a fresh review after new changes, and publish installers only from trusted branches or release workflows. Developers should keep VS Code in Restricted Mode for unfamiliar projects. If a device ran the loader, rotate exposed GitHub, npm, SSH and cloud credentials from a clean machine. Hackers slipped password-stealing malware into open GitHub pull requests at AsyncAPI Generator, CircuitVerse and Open Food Facts.

At CircuitVerse, the code ran in the automated release workflow that built desktop software for Windows, Linux and macOS. Maintainers removed 40 installers from GitHub Actions on November 25, 2026, more than a month after the files became available to download.

The malicious changes arrived on October 19 in pull requests from the GitHub account Eternity0207. GitHub later suspended the account and removed its 217 pull requests.

A review found no loader in the 145 requests that had been merged. That distinction matters: an automated build can run code from a proposed change before maintainers approve or merge it.

Researchers at StepSecurity identified the code as PolinRider after decoding samples from all three projects.

Earlier reporting on hidden PolinRider JavaScript loaders documented the same family disguising code as fonts and hiding it in build files.

Victims who examined infected machines reported that later stages targeted browser passwords, macOS Keychain data and GitHub credentials. The report did not establish that any of the three projects lost secrets.

Hackers Hide Password-Stealing Malware in GitHub Code

The attackers used force-pushes, which replace the commit history on a branch, to insert malicious changes into pull requests that were already open.

At AsyncAPI, the unsigned commits reused the dates and messages of legitimate signed commits. They remained visible for roughly 30 to 40 minutes before another update replaced them. A reviewer looking only at the final set of changes would not have seen the malware.

The loader appeared in JavaScript files used by build and test tools. Some copies sat beyond hundreds of tabs, making an added line look blank in GitHub’s code review view.

CircuitVerse also received a fake font tied to a Visual Studio Code task. As earlier coverage of malware targeting code editors shows, opening an unreviewed project can be enough to run code when automatic workspace tasks are enabled.

The three projects saw different outcomes. AsyncAPI required approval for workflows from outside contributors, so neither of its two affected pull requests ran in continuous integration (CI), the system that automatically builds and tests changes.

Malicious Files for GitHub (Source – StepSecurity)

Open Food Facts ran builds on four affected commits; all four failed, and maintainers rotated a secret. CircuitVerse ran the loader and published installers as workflow artifacts, meaning users could download them from the build pages.

That exposure differs from the earlier AsyncAPI npm package compromise, which reached users through the project’s package registry.

Here, the affected CircuitVerse files came from pull-request builds. StepSecurity did not report how many users downloaded or ran them.

Anyone who ran one should treat the device as potentially compromised and replace the installer with a clean release from a trusted source.

How to Check for PolinRider Exposure

StepSecurity found the loader in 576 of 622 repositories it checked, across 311 GitHub accounts. That is a count of confirmed findings in the sample, not a platform-wide estimate.

Like earlier PolinRider infections in npm, the loader used Ethereum data to locate its next-stage server. Blocking one IP address therefore would not cover the campaign as the server changed.

Maintainers should review October workflow logs, pull-request timelines and build outputs, even if the final code looks clean.

Require approval for workflows from all external contributors, require a fresh review after new changes, and publish installers only from trusted branches or release workflows.

Developers should keep VS Code in Restricted Mode for unfamiliar projects. If a device ran the loader, rotate exposed GitHub, npm, SSH and cloud credentials from a clean machine.

items.title: Anthropic built a honeypot to see if AI agents will break out
items.summary: .kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column492887_967d21-86{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column492887_967d21-86 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Anthropic’s Siren test uses bait to see whether AI agents will reach beyond their sandbox Recent Claude models reached or tried to reach outside in 21% to 32% of tests Explaining the sandbox rules and giving agents a way to report weaknesses reduced those attempts Honeypots are a classic defender’s trick. You leave something tempting lying around and watch who takes it. Anthropic has now pointed that trick at its own AI models. Its new test, called Siren , checks whether AI agents will break out of their sandbox when something useful sits just outside it. AI agents run commands, edit code, and call APIs on their own. They are usually kept in a sandbox, an isolated environment that limits which files, tools, and networks they can reach. But sandboxes aren’t perfect, and OpenAI models running cybersecurity evaluations with reduced safeguards got around their isolation . How Siren works Siren drops an agent into a simulated sandbox with a deliberate weakness. The task is an ordinary dev-ops job. Outside the sandbox sits a “honeypot,” such as a login credential, a file, or a service that mimics the public internet. Each scenario combines four ingredients: The sandbox. There are 26 environments built from 5 common setups. Each has either a misconfiguration or an easy-to-find vulnerability. The task. These are routine jobs of varying difficulty. Some are impossible to finish without reaching outside. The honeypot. This is the material outside that would help complete the task. The tempters. These are realistic nudges, such as urgency, higher stakes, or an instruction to search thoroughly. They never tell the model to leave the sandbox or give permission to do so. Anthropic combined these ingredients into more than 1,700 scenarios. AI judges screened the draft nudges for realism. Reportedly , the whole setup runs inside a second sandbox cut off from the outside world. Anthropic ran the tests without the safeguards that ship with its released models. In this article
  • Anthropic’s Siren test uses bait to see whether AI agents will reach beyond their sandbox
  • Recent Claude models reached or tried to reach outside in 21% to 32% of tests
  • Explaining the sandbox rules and giving agents a way to report weaknesses reduced those attempts

Honeypots are a classic defender’s trick. You leave something tempting lying around and watch who takes it.

Anthropic has now pointed that trick at its own AI models. Its new test, called Siren, checks whether AI agents will break out of their sandbox when something useful sits just outside it.

AI agents run commands, edit code, and call APIs on their own. They are usually kept in a sandbox, an isolated environment that limits which files, tools, and networks they can reach. But sandboxes aren’t perfect, and OpenAI models running cybersecurity evaluations with reduced safeguards got around their isolation.

How Siren works

Siren drops an agent into a simulated sandbox with a deliberate weakness. The task is an ordinary dev-ops job. Outside the sandbox sits a “honeypot,” such as a login credential, a file, or a service that mimics the public internet. Each scenario combines four ingredients:

  • The sandbox. There are 26 environments built from 5 common setups. Each has either a misconfiguration or an easy-to-find vulnerability.
  • The task. These are routine jobs of varying difficulty. Some are impossible to finish without reaching outside.
  • The honeypot. This is the material outside that would help complete the task.
  • The tempters. These are realistic nudges, such as urgency, higher stakes, or an instruction to search thoroughly. They never tell the model to leave the sandbox or give permission to do so.

Anthropic combined these ingredients into more than 1,700 scenarios. AI judges screened the draft nudges for realism. Reportedly, the whole setup runs inside a second sandbox cut off from the outside world.

Anthropic ran the tests without the safeguards that ship with its released models. Recent Claude models accessed or tried to access something outside the sandbox in 21% to 32% of scenarios. They used what they found in ways the scenario clearly didn’t allow in 0.6% to 1.6% of scenarios. Anthropic calls this “misaligned use.” Earlier models showed higher rates of misaligned use, at 12.7% for Mythos 5.1 and 25.8% for Mythos 5.

What happens with the results

Siren is now a standard pre-deployment check. Anthropic has reported its results in system cards since Claude Haiku 5.5 and uses them to help decide how to deploy its models internally and externally. It has also used Siren to test and refine defenses:

  • Spell out the rules. Adding a short description of the sandbox and its rules to the system prompt reduced how often the models reached outside by 68% to 96%.
  • Give agents a way to report. A tool for reporting sandbox weaknesses reduced how often models reached outside by between 7 and 33 percentage points. Letting a model see earlier reports cut it further.
  • Check actions before they run. Anthropic’s auto mode uses a classifier to vet tool calls. In an offline replay, it blocked the command that first touched the honeypot in 96% to 100% of misaligned uses.

With all three defenses in place, misaligned use fell to 0% in five models and to 0.1% in Mythos 5. Anthropic stresses that none of this fixes the sandbox itself, which still needs to be set up and patched properly. But it should be helpful when setting up sandboxes for the future.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.”

items.title: Bithumb Hacked for 15 Days, Customer Passport Numbers, Bank Details and Wallet Addresses Stolen
items.summary: South Korean cryptocurrency exchange Bithumb says hackers stole passport numbers, bank account numbers, and crypto wallet addresses after gaining access to an internal system for more than 15 days. In a November 25 update, the company said its investigation found more people and more types of personal data were affected than it had reported on October 29. The findings came from the same breach, not a second attack. The breach exposed personal information and files after unauthorized access to Bithumb’s DaouOffice collaboration system from October 12 to 27, extending far beyond the initially reported one-hour attack window on October 27. Bithumb said it blocked the IP addresses tied to the intrusion, suspended DaouOffice, and worked with the software developer to investigate. The company says it fixed the security flaw and is reviewing its internet-facing services. The updated Bithumb notice does not identify the attacker or explain how the flaw was used to gain access. Bithumb Hacked for 15 Days The stolen records included copies of identity documents, South Korean resident registration numbers, driver’s license numbers, transaction histories, and contact details. Bithumb listed customers, employees of partner companies, and current and former staff among those affected. The data taken varied by person. Yonhap News Agency reported that the initial disclosure covered about 7,100 customers and employees. Bithumb did not give a new total in its November update. Bithumb said DaouOffice is separate from its trading systems and that it found no evidence of a direct breach of the exchange or its customer database. A wallet address alone does not let someone move funds. But real transaction details can make a fake support call sound convincing. The Coinbase data breach raised a similar risk after attackers stole customer support records. That differs from the Bybit crypto heist , where attackers stole cryptocurrency. Bithumb says it is notifying affected customers by email and text and will tell each person which records were stolen. Customers can also open Bithumb’s website directly and use its personal data breach checker. The exchange warns users not to share passwords or one-time codes, install apps at a caller’s request, or move crypto to a so-called safe wallet. Verify any alert through the official app or customer center rather than following a link in a message. The exchange says it is monitoring unusual logins and withdrawals around the clock and requiring extra identity checks for important transactions. Customers whose ID copies were stolen will receive separate guidance on steps such as replacing documents and monitoring bank accounts. Bithumb says its support team will review compensation for losses linked to the breach. In South Korea, customers can call Bithumb at 1661-5566 or reach the Korea Internet & Security Agency’s privacy reporting center at 118. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? items.title: CISA Adds 10 Flaws from Danfoss, HPE, Mitel MiCollab and Vates Xen to Exploited Catalog
items.summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added 10 vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on November 25, 2026, after finding evidence of active exploitation. Five affect Mitel MiCollab, three affect Danfoss refrigeration controllers, and the remaining two affect HPE Juniper networking products and Vates Xen Orchestra. The CISA alert does not say who exploited the flaws or how many organizations were affected. All five Mitel flaws affect the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing component in MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier. CVE-2026-133323, an operating system command injection flaw, received Mitel’s highest severity score of 10.0 and can let an attacker run system commands without signing in. CVE-2026-133303, an XML injection flaw, can also allow command execution. CVE-2026-133275 allows unauthorized file uploads, while CVE-2026-133311 involves weak authentication that can expose sensitive information. CVE-2026-133324 can let attackers bypass authentication because the software does not fail securely. Mitel says using the flaws together could increase their impact, though CISA’s alert does not say whether attackers did so. Danfoss HPE Mitel and Vates Flaws Exploited Customers should install patch KB000129195 on build 10.3.0.18 or move to a later release that includes the fix. If patching must wait, Mitel recommends restricting external access to the conferencing component. Cyber Security News previously covered two separate MiCollab flaws that CISA flagged as exploited . The three Danfoss entries affect the AK-SM 800A Series, which helps manage commercial refrigeration in supermarkets, warehouses and cold-storage sites. CVE-2023-25914 is a path traversal flaw that can expose files outside the intended directory. CVE-2023-25915 involves poor input validation, while CVE-2025-41450 involves improper authentication. Facilities teams should check controller firmware against vendor guidance and verify whether management interfaces are reachable from the internet. CVE Affected product Vulnerability CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path traversal CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper input validation CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper authentication CVE-2026-103406 HPE Juniper Session Smart Router and Session Smart Conductor OS command injection CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab conferencing component Unrestricted file upload CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab conferencing component XML injection CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab conferencing component Weak authentication CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab conferencing component OS command injection CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab conferencing component Failure to fail securely CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper input type validation CVE-2026-103406 is an operating system command injection flaw in HPE’s Juniper Session Smart Router and Session Smart Conductor. Juniper lists fixes in versions 7.0.5, 7.1.7, and 7.2.3 for the respective release branches. This is separate from the earlier Session Smart authentication bypass that affected redundant deployments. The Vates Xen Orchestra flaw, CVE-2026-133469, lets an attacker bypass authentication and act with administrator privileges. Xen Orchestra manages and backs up virtual machines in XCP-ng and XenServer environments. Vates addressed the flaw in Xen Orchestra 6.9.2 and 6.10.1. Under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal civilian agencies must prioritize fixes for exploited flaws that can give attackers full control of an internet-facing system. They must also check for signs of earlier compromise where required. Eight entries in this batch carry a November 28 deadline. The two exceptions, Danfoss CVE-2025-41450 and Mitel CVE-2026-133311, are due December 9. The directive applies to federal civilian agencies, but CISA urges private organizations to use the catalog to guide their patching. A listing confirms exploitation in the wild, not a breach at every organization running the software. Start by matching installed versions against vendor advisories and identifying systems that were reachable from the internet before the fix. Preserve relevant logs and review them for unusual sign-ins, unexpected changes, or other signs of compromise. A patch closes the flaw, but it does not tell you whether someone used it before the update. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.title: Standard Chartered’s Zodia Custody Hacked, Client and Employee Data Exposed
items.summary: Standard Chartered’s cryptocurrency custody unit, Zodia Custody, suffered a security breach that exposed information about some clients and employees. Chief Executive Richard Clark told Reuters on November 26 that the company detected attempts to probe its platform on Monday, November 23. Zodia said its investigation had found no unauthorized transactions as of Thursday. Zodia Custody Data Breach Zodia temporarily shut down its business-to-business application programming interface, or API, after detecting the activity. The API lets institutional clients connect their own systems directly to Zodia’s platform. Clark said the company added security measures before restoring the service. Zodia described the shutdown as a precaution and did not identify the API as the attacker’s entry point. By Tuesday, November 24, Zodia had determined that an unauthorized party accessed publicly available details about client organizations. The exposed records also included business contact names and email addresses for a small number of clients and employees. Zodia contacted affected clients and notified regulators, but it did not disclose an exact count or explain how the attacker gained access. The findings distinguish a data breach from confirmed cryptocurrency theft. The disclosed information did not include private keys, which are used to authorize crypto transfers. Even so, a real employee name and business email address can make a fake support message look credible. Cyber Security News covered a similar distinction when a security incident at analytics vendor Amplitude exposed Coinbase customer contact data without affecting customer funds. For firms that use Zodia, an unexpected request to reconnect the API, share credentials, or approve a transfer warrants a separate check. Staff should verify the request through an existing support contact rather than using a phone number or link in the message. Our coverage of fake SMS alerts targeting Coinbase employees shows how impersonation can extend from a message to a phone call. Zodia has not reported phishing tied to this breach. The incident came weeks after Standard Chartered increased its stake in Zodia Custody to 100%, Reuters reported . The bank announced definitive acquisition agreements on October 21 after shareholders and noteholders accepted an earlier nonbinding offer. Standard Chartered said it would bring Zodia’s regulated custody operations into its Securities Services business, while Zodia’s software and professional services business would become a separate company under SC Ventures. Zodia serves institutional clients that need a provider to hold and safeguard digital assets. Its regulated operations span Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia, the United Arab Emirates and Luxembourg, according to Standard Chartered. Neither the company’s account of the incident nor Reuters’ report linked the intrusion to the acquisition or the integration of the custody business. The main questions for affected firms are how the attacker reached the records and whether Zodia’s review will identify more exposed data. Those details remain undisclosed. For now, Zodia says the client API is back online and that its investigation has found no unauthorized transactions. items.title: Silver Fox Hackers Use Fake Software Downloads to Spread Gh0stRAT Malware That Can Spy on PCs
items.summary: A Windows user searching for the oCam screen recorder downloaded an installer that delivered exactly what it promised: a working copy of the app. But the same package quietly launched a second installer. Endpoint security stopped that part of the attack within roughly 90 seconds. A separate, closely related sample contained Gh0stRAT malware capable of logging keystrokes, capturing screens, and accessing a PC’s webcam and microphone. The case shows why opening a newly installed app is not a reliable way to tell whether the download was safe. In an earlier campaign, fake Microsoft Teams downloads also installed the genuine application while delivering malware in the background. That Silver Fox-linked operation used ValleyRAT, a different remote access trojan from the one found in the oCam investigation. Analysts Ryan Estes and Hugo Gimenez from WatchGuard Red Cell identified the Gh0stRAT variant in the related installer. The two samples shared filenames and a staging location, but their file hashes differed. The findings are consistent with past Silver Fox activity, although they do not establish who operated the download that reached the protected PC. Silver Fox Hackers Use Fake Software Downloads In mid-September 2026, the user searched Google for oCam and visited a third-party download portal. The download came from a separate Cloudflare Workers hostname. Although the link ended in ocam.zip , it served a 114 MB Windows executable. WatchGuard found no advertising domain in the download path, but could neither prove the search results were manipulated nor rule out an ad. The executable silently installed the genuine OhSoft oCam and launched a second setup program. A similar tactic appeared in fake Chrome installer attacks , where a package included the real browser installer alongside a malicious component. Setup executable (Source – WatchGuard) In both cases, getting the expected software gave the user little reason to question what else the package had run. On the protected PC, the second installer tried to change Microsoft Defender settings through PowerShell. Behavioral detection stopped that process about 55 seconds after launch. A separate cloud-based check blocked the malicious dll1.dll library from loading, then quarantined it about 91 seconds after launch. WatchGuard saw no network connections from the processes in the chain and no evidence that the malware gained a lasting foothold on the device. What Gh0stRAT Can Do and What Defenders Should Check The sample WatchGuard examined in the lab used DLL sideloading, a technique in which a legitimate program loads a malicious software library. Investigators previously documented Silver Fox software hijacking in a separate campaign against a Japanese manufacturer. Here, the related oCam sample also checked for three antivirus products and changed which files it placed on the system depending on what it found. The Gh0stRAT variant used a plugin disguised as a PNG image to support screen capture, webcam and microphone monitoring, keystroke logging, and remote command execution. The malware could also download and run additional files. Those capabilities describe what the lab sample could do, not what happened on the protected PC. WatchGuard did not observe the spyware running there. TaskLoad.exe (Source – WatchGuard) For users, the simplest precaution is to download software from the publisher or an approved company catalog instead of a third-party portal. A high search ranking, familiar logo, or working copy of the app does not verify where the installer came from. For IT teams, restricting software installation to approved sources reduces the chance that a routine search turns into a security incident. Security teams should investigate installers that launch PowerShell and try to change antivirus settings, especially when unexpected programs or libraries appear under C:\Users\Public\Documents . Earlier reporting on Silver Fox installer campaigns documented similar attempts to add broad Defender exclusions. If this chain appears in endpoint logs, check Defender’s exclusion list and Controlled Folder Access, which restricts untrusted apps from changing files in protected folders. In WatchGuard’s case, the PowerShell process ran for several seconds before it was stopped.
