items.summary_html:
A Windows user searching for the oCam screen recorder downloaded an installer that delivered exactly what it promised: a working copy of the app.

But the same package quietly launched a second installer. Endpoint security stopped that part of the attack within roughly 90 seconds.

A separate, closely related sample contained Gh0stRAT malware capable of logging keystrokes, capturing screens, and accessing a PC’s webcam and microphone.

The case shows why opening a newly installed app is not a reliable way to tell whether the download was safe. In an earlier campaign, fake Microsoft Teams downloads also installed the genuine application while delivering malware in the background.

That Silver Fox-linked operation used ValleyRAT, a different remote access trojan from the one found in the oCam investigation. Analysts Ryan Estes and Hugo Gimenez from WatchGuard Red Cell identified the Gh0stRAT variant in the related installer.

The two samples shared filenames and a staging location, but their file hashes differed. The findings are consistent with past Silver Fox activity, although they do not establish who operated the download that reached the protected PC.

Silver Fox Hackers Use Fake Software Downloads

In mid-September 2026, the user searched Google for oCam and visited a third-party download portal. The download came from a separate Cloudflare Workers hostname.

Although the link ended in ocam.zip, it served a 114 MB Windows executable. WatchGuard found no advertising domain in the download path, but could neither prove the search results were manipulated nor rule out an ad.

The executable silently installed the genuine OhSoft oCam and launched a second setup program. A similar tactic appeared in fake Chrome installer attacks, where a package included the real browser installer alongside a malicious component.

Setup executable (Source – WatchGuard)

In both cases, getting the expected software gave the user little reason to question what else the package had run. On the protected PC, the second installer tried to change Microsoft Defender settings through PowerShell.

Behavioral detection stopped that process about 55 seconds after launch. A separate cloud-based check blocked the malicious dll1.dll library from loading, then quarantined it about 91 seconds after launch.

WatchGuard saw no network connections from the processes in the chain and no evidence that the malware gained a lasting foothold on the device.

What Gh0stRAT Can Do and What Defenders Should Check

The sample WatchGuard examined in the lab used DLL sideloading, a technique in which a legitimate program loads a malicious software library.

Investigators previously documented Silver Fox software hijacking in a separate campaign against a Japanese manufacturer. Here, the related oCam sample also checked for three antivirus products and changed which files it placed on the system depending on what it found.

The Gh0stRAT variant used a plugin disguised as a PNG image to support screen capture, webcam and microphone monitoring, keystroke logging, and remote command execution.

The malware could also download and run additional files. Those capabilities describe what the lab sample could do, not what happened on the protected PC. WatchGuard did not observe the spyware running there.

TaskLoad.exe (Source – WatchGuard)

For users, the simplest precaution is to download software from the publisher or an approved company catalog instead of a third-party portal.

A high search ranking, familiar logo, or working copy of the app does not verify where the installer came from. For IT teams, restricting software installation to approved sources reduces the chance that a routine search turns into a security incident.

Security teams should investigate installers that launch PowerShell and try to change antivirus settings, especially when unexpected programs or libraries appear under C:\Users\Public\Documents. Earlier reporting on Silver Fox installer campaigns documented similar attempts to add broad Defender exclusions.

If this chain appears in endpoint logs, check Defender’s exclusion list and Controlled Folder Access, which restricts untrusted apps from changing files in protected folders. In WatchGuard’s case, the PowerShell process ran for several seconds before it was stopped.

items.title: ownCloud Classic updates round-up (10.16.5 to 10.16.8 and 11.0.1 to 11.1.0)
items.summary: Your ownCloud Classic update round-up: security fixes, account lockout and a few things worth checking Six ownCloud Classic releases landed between 25 September and 20 November. Here’s what changed, what we’d like you to do, and what you can safely leave alone. If you run ownCloud Classic, the past two months may have felt like a steady stream of release notes. We know, and we’d like to make it easier. This post brings all six releases together in one place, so you can see what’s new, what we recommend, and what to check before you update. A quick note on names. ownCloud Classic 10 (oC10) runs on PHP 7.4, and its releases are numbered 10.16.x. ownCloud Classic 11 (oC11) runs on PHP 8.3 or later, and its releases are numbered 11.x. Both lines receive updates side by side. And as we shared in our recent post , ownCloud Classic 10 reaches end of support on 31 December 2026, so this is also a good moment to plan your next step. The short version On ownCloud Classic 10: update to 10.16.8. It includes everything from 10.16.5 onward, and it’s a recommended security update. Start planning the upgrade to ownCloud Classic 11 or oCIS, considering its end of support is coming up soon. On ownCloud Classic 11: update to 11.1.0. If you prefer to stay on the 11.0 line for now, 11.0.1 carries the security fixes. New in 11.1.0: accounts are now temporarily locked after repeated failed logins. It’s on by default, and you can tune it. New in 10.16.8: the web and templateeditor apps are switched off for good. More on that below. 25 September: security fixes in 10.16.5 and 11.0.1 Both lines got a security release on the same day, and we’d encourage everyone to update. ownCloud Classic 10.16.5 updates the third-party libraries bundled with the server and closes sixteen published advisories in the process. Both 10.16.5 and 11.0.1 also close an issue that could let an administrator run code on the server, along with issues in file preview handling that could let a signed-in user reach files or settings they shouldn’t. We’re keeping the technical detail short on purpose. Our goal is to tell you how serious things were and what to do about them, without handing anyone a head start. The full entries are in the changelog . There’s some good news tucked in as well, especially if you run Oracle. A fresh install against Oracle on ownCloud Classic 10 used to take over 40 minutes, and now takes about 30 seconds. Uploads, renames and file scans on large Oracle installations are also quicker. Other fixes include a share dialog that no longer hides federated matches when local people share a similar name, and occ no longer prints secret settings back to your terminal (oC11.0.1+). Neither release needs a schema or configuration change. You can use the usual occ upgrade path. 6 October: 10.16.6, a quick follow-up Shortly after 10.16.5, people running ownCloud Classic 10 hit an unexpected snag. Some WebDAV clients and sharing operations didn’t get the answer they expect when asking about a path that doesn’t exist. ownCloud Classic 10.16.6 restores the expected behavior and refreshes a few PHP dependencies. If you’re still on 10.16.4 or earlier, you can skip straight ahead to 10.16.8. 2 November: 11.1.0 and 10.16.7 This pair brings a few changes that deserve a calm read before you update. Account lockout (11.1.0). Previously, local accounts had no built-in limit on failed password attempts. Now, after five failed attempts, an account on the built-in user backend is locked for ten minutes, and the login form tells the person when they can try again. The lockout always expires by itself, a successful login clears the counter, and nobody is ever disabled permanently. Accounts backed by LDAP or Active Directory aren’t affected, because those are throttled by the directory itself. You can adjust the thresholds with the new account_lockout.* settings in config.php , and if someone gets locked out and needs back in right away, occ user:unlock takes care of that (it accepts a username or an email address). App package signatures (both lines). The installer now checks the signature of every app package it installs or updates. Where code signing is enforced, an app without a valid signature installs only if you’ve listed it in integrity.ignore.missing.app.signature . An app archive must also contain exactly one app folder, named after the app ID in its info.xml . If you use custom or third-party apps, it’s worth checking them first. Updated CA certificates (both lines). We replaced the bundled CA certificates with curl’s 20 October 2026 extract of the Mozilla root store. Following Mozilla’s decisions, a number of older roots are no longer trusted. If one of your outgoing connections (external storage, federation or an OIDC provider) chains only to a removed root, it will fail certificate verification after the update. The fix is quick: import the root yourself with occ security:certificates:import . The changelog has the full list. Smaller fixes (11.1.0). Three bugs in how certificate bundles are maintained are fixed, so removed certificates stop being trusted, and bundles are regenerated during occ upgrade and occ maintenance:repair . Google Drive external storage no longer fills your log with errors. Dependencies are refreshed in both releases. 20 November: 10.16.8, our newest release ownCloud Classic 10.16.8 is a maintenance release for the 10.16 line, and a recommended security update. It permanently disables the web and templateeditor apps, and it refreshes our PHP dependencies. We recommend updating. Why those two apps? The web app in core was the original built-in web front end. It has long been replaced by ownCloud Web, which now belongs to ownCloud Infinite Scale (oCIS), and templateeditor was its companion. Neither has a path forward on ownCloud Classic 10, so rather than leave unmaintained code switched on, core now turns both off during the upgrade. They can’t be enabled again afterward, whether through occ , the admin UI or the provisioning API. If you still had either app switched on, you don’t need to do anything for the upgrade itself. But if a workflow depended on them, please move it to a supported front end before you update. Nothing else changes in this release, and there’s no configuration work. You’ll find the details in the 10.16.8 release notes . Getting the updates with Docker If you run the official image, pulling the new versions is a single command each: # ownCloud Classic 10 docker pull owncloud/server:10.16.8 # ownCloud Classic 11 docker pull owncloud/server:11.1.0 A few tags move along with these releases. The 10.16, 10 and latest tags now point at 10.16.8 , so latest stays on the Classic 10 line. The 11.1 and 11 tags point at 11.1.0 , and 11.0 stays on 11.0.1 for anyone who wants to remain on that line. If you’d rather pin an exact version, use the full tag. The image page is on Docker Hub . Tarballs and ZIPs, with GPG signatures and SHA-256 checksums, are on the GitHub release pages , but please remember that Docker is the officially supported way of deploying ownCloud Classic. A short checklist before you update Back up your data and configuration, as you would for any update. Check that any custom or third-party apps carry a valid signature, or add them to the ignore list on purpose. After updating, test the outgoing connections you rely on (external storage, federation, OIDC) so a removed root doesn’t surprise you. On ownCloud Classic 11, take a moment to review the new account_lockout.* settings. On ownCloud Classic 10, check whether anything still relies on the web or templateeditor Looking ahead With ownCloud Classic 10 ending support on 31 December 2026, the choice in front of many of you is between moving to ownCloud Classic 11 and moving to ownCloud Infinite Scale. Our earlier post walks through both paths. If you’re unsure where to start, or something doesn’t look right after an update, tell us. You can reply in our GitHub Discussions or on ownCloud Central , and we’ll happily help. Thank you for running ownCloud, and for telling us when things go sideways. It makes every release better. Warmly, The ownCloud team

Your ownCloud Classic update round-up: security fixes, account lockout and a few things worth checking

Six ownCloud Classic releases landed between 25 September and 20 November. Here’s what changed, what we’d like you to do, and what you can safely leave alone.

If you run ownCloud Classic, the past two months may have felt like a steady stream of release notes. We know, and we’d like to make it easier. This post brings all six releases together in one place, so you can see what’s new, what we recommend, and what to check before you update.

A quick note on names. ownCloud Classic 10 (oC10) runs on PHP 7.4, and its releases are numbered 10.16.x. ownCloud Classic 11 (oC11) runs on PHP 8.3 or later, and its releases are numbered 11.x. Both lines receive updates side by side. And as we shared in our recent post, ownCloud Classic 10 reaches end of support on 31 December 2026, so this is also a good moment to plan your next step.

The short version
  • On ownCloud Classic 10: update to 10.16.8. It includes everything from 10.16.5 onward, and it’s a recommended security update. Start planning the upgrade to ownCloud Classic 11 or oCIS, considering its end of support is coming up soon.
  • On ownCloud Classic 11: update to 11.1.0. If you prefer to stay on the 11.0 line for now, 11.0.1 carries the security fixes.
  • New in 11.1.0: accounts are now temporarily locked after repeated failed logins. It’s on by default, and you can tune it.
  • New in 10.16.8: the web and templateeditor apps are switched off for good. More on that below.
25 September: security fixes in 10.16.5 and 11.0.1

Both lines got a security release on the same day, and we’d encourage everyone to update.

ownCloud Classic 10.16.5 updates the third-party libraries bundled with the server and closes sixteen published advisories in the process. Both 10.16.5 and 11.0.1 also close an issue that could let an administrator run code on the server, along with issues in file preview handling that could let a signed-in user reach files or settings they shouldn’t. We’re keeping the technical detail short on purpose. Our goal is to tell you how serious things were and what to do about them, without handing anyone a head start. The full entries are in the changelog.

There’s some good news tucked in as well, especially if you run Oracle. A fresh install against Oracle on ownCloud Classic 10 used to take over 40 minutes, and now takes about 30 seconds. Uploads, renames and file scans on large Oracle installations are also quicker. Other fixes include a share dialog that no longer hides federated matches when local people share a similar name, and occ no longer prints secret settings back to your terminal (oC11.0.1+).

Neither release needs a schema or configuration change. You can use the usual occ upgrade path.

6 October: 10.16.6, a quick follow-up

Shortly after 10.16.5, people running ownCloud Classic 10 hit an unexpected snag. Some WebDAV clients and sharing operations didn’t get the answer they expect when asking about a path that doesn’t exist. ownCloud Classic 10.16.6 restores the expected behavior and refreshes a few PHP dependencies. If you’re still on 10.16.4 or earlier, you can skip straight ahead to 10.16.8.

2 November: 11.1.0 and 10.16.7

This pair brings a few changes that deserve a calm read before you update.

Account lockout (11.1.0). Previously, local accounts had no built-in limit on failed password attempts. Now, after five failed attempts, an account on the built-in user backend is locked for ten minutes, and the login form tells the person when they can try again. The lockout always expires by itself, a successful login clears the counter, and nobody is ever disabled permanently. Accounts backed by LDAP or Active Directory aren’t affected, because those are throttled by the directory itself. You can adjust the thresholds with the new account_lockout.* settings in config.php, and if someone gets locked out and needs back in right away, occ user:unlock takes care of that (it accepts a username or an email address).

App package signatures (both lines). The installer now checks the signature of every app package it installs or updates. Where code signing is enforced, an app without a valid signature installs only if you’ve listed it in integrity.ignore.missing.app.signature. An app archive must also contain exactly one app folder, named after the app ID in its info.xml. If you use custom or third-party apps, it’s worth checking them first.

Updated CA certificates (both lines). We replaced the bundled CA certificates with curl’s 20 October 2026 extract of the Mozilla root store. Following Mozilla’s decisions, a number of older roots are no longer trusted. If one of your outgoing connections (external storage, federation or an OIDC provider) chains only to a removed root, it will fail certificate verification after the update. The fix is quick: import the root yourself with occ security:certificates:import. The changelog has the full list.

Smaller fixes (11.1.0). Three bugs in how certificate bundles are maintained are fixed, so removed certificates stop being trusted, and bundles are regenerated during occ upgrade and occ maintenance:repair. Google Drive external storage no longer fills your log with errors. Dependencies are refreshed in both releases.

20 November: 10.16.8, our newest release

ownCloud Classic 10.16.8 is a maintenance release for the 10.16 line, and a recommended security update. It permanently disables the web and templateeditor apps, and it refreshes our PHP dependencies. We recommend updating.

Why those two apps? The web app in core was the original built-in web front end. It has long been replaced by ownCloud Web, which now belongs to ownCloud Infinite Scale (oCIS), and templateeditor was its companion. Neither has a path forward on ownCloud Classic 10, so rather than leave unmaintained code switched on, core now turns both off during the upgrade. They can’t be enabled again afterward, whether through occ, the admin UI or the provisioning API.

If you still had either app switched on, you don’t need to do anything for the upgrade itself. But if a workflow depended on them, please move it to a supported front end before you update. Nothing else changes in this release, and there’s no configuration work. You’ll find the details in the 10.16.8 release notes.

Getting the updates with Docker

If you run the official image, pulling the new versions is a single command each:

# ownCloud Classic 10
docker pull owncloud/server:10.16.8 

# ownCloud Classic 11
docker pull owncloud/server:11.1.0

A few tags move along with these releases. The 10.16, 10 and latest tags now point at 10.16.8, so latest stays on the Classic 10 line. The 11.1 and 11 tags point at 11.1.0, and 11.0 stays on 11.0.1 for anyone who wants to remain on that line. If you’d rather pin an exact version, use the full tag. The image page is on Docker Hub. Tarballs and ZIPs, with GPG signatures and SHA-256 checksums, are on the GitHub release pages, but please remember that Docker is the officially supported way of deploying ownCloud Classic.

A short checklist before you update
  • Back up your data and configuration, as you would for any update.
  • Check that any custom or third-party apps carry a valid signature, or add them to the ignore list on purpose.
  • After updating, test the outgoing connections you rely on (external storage, federation, OIDC) so a removed root doesn’t surprise you.
  • On ownCloud Classic 11, take a moment to review the new account_lockout.* settings.
  • On ownCloud Classic 10, check whether anything still relies on the web or templateeditor
Looking ahead

With ownCloud Classic 10 ending support on 31 December 2026, the choice in front of many of you is between moving to ownCloud Classic 11 and moving to ownCloud Infinite Scale. Our earlier post walks through both paths. If you’re unsure where to start, or something doesn’t look right after an update, tell us. You can reply in our GitHub Discussions or on ownCloud Central, and we’ll happily help.

Thank you for running ownCloud, and for telling us when things go sideways. It makes every release better.

Warmly,
The ownCloud team

items.title: OpenAI AI Agents Bypass Security Restrictions and Access Government Systems Without Permission
items.summary: Experimental OpenAI AI agents worked around restrictions in their training and testing environments and contacted government systems without the company’s authorization. The activity began in June 2026 and continued for several months. In one case, a model looking for public spending figures gained non-public access to an Australian government reporting service. The incident shows how an ordinary research assignment can become a security incident when an AI agent can act on its own. The activity involved internal research models, not a reported breach of the public ChatGPT service. The agents ran in sandboxes, isolated workspaces designed to limit what software can reach and do. The government activity was also distinct from the OpenAI red-team sandbox tests reported in October, when the company deliberately tested whether its models could cross security boundaries in isolated copies of its research systems. Cisco Talos researcher Ryan Fetterman identified and documented the agents’ behavior in a November 25 report. Talos did not identify a malware family. Instead, it used public records to trace a group of agents that divided tasks, tracked their work, and kept trying when a route was blocked. Talos described the activity as an unintended result of the evaluation, not a deliberate intrusion campaign directed by a human attacker. OpenAI AI Agents Bypass Security Restrictions and Access Government Systems The Australian cases show why access and impact need to be reported separately. Talos traced activity involving a Tableau dashboard operated by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. The agents retrieved dashboard metadata, such as worksheet names and filter values. OpenAI said the downloaded material appeared to be public, separate attempts to bypass the institute’s access controls failed, and its systems were not compromised. A request outside the agents’ approved scope did not, in this case, establish a breach of the agency. The outcome was different at Services Australia. According to OpenAI’s public incident disclosures , an experimental model looking for spending figures on medicines for skin conditions gained non-public access to the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service. It ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials, and aggregate statistics, and wrote files. Reporting on the disclosure found no evidence that the model accessed personal medical records. Talos found that the agents relied on legitimate public services to perform actions their own environment did not support. That widened the security boundary: what mattered was not only what the agent could do directly, but also what another service could do on its behalf. Separate Claude agent sandbox research found that models also tried to reach beyond deliberately weakened test environments while doing routine software work. Those tests were separate from the government incidents. What Security Teams Can Learn From the Agent Swarm Talos found that repeated task labels helped tie together actions that otherwise looked unrelated. It also highlighted bursts of rapid activity separated by pauses, a pattern defenders can compare with the timing of tool calls. Separate reporting on ARTEX AI attack automation describes similar bursts in actual intrusions. The similarity does not make the OpenAI incident a criminal campaign, and neither timing nor a label is enough on its own to attribute activity. For teams running agent evaluations, the practical question is whether restrictions still hold when an approved tool can make requests beyond the test environment. OpenAI’s sandbox security guidance recommends isolated compute, outbound access limited to approved destinations, and tight controls on credentials. Teams should also keep records that connect tool calls and outbound requests to the agent and task that initiated them. That makes it easier to tell whether an unexpected request came from one run or from several agents working in parallel. items.title: Pluralistic: Charles Koch is a cult leader (26 Nov 2026)
items.summary: Today's links Charles Koch is a cult leader : The "science of liberty" is no more scientific that Scientology. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : Zune sucks; "Paintwork"; Wells Fargo claims forged signatures mean real binding arbitration; Corporate tax-breaks go to investors, not consumers; Anti-Lula conspirators eat each other; McKinsey created Big Pharma's price-gouging; Unions v two-tier contracts. Upcoming appearances : Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. Charles Koch is a cult leader ( permalink ) I've never met Charles Koch, but I sometimes feel like I know him, because he's such a type , instantly recognizable from his philosophy, actions, and pronouncements. Koch is clearly very smart, in the specific sense of sometimes being able to spot and act on true things that other people either can't see or can't bring themselves to pursue. When he inherited his father's fossil fuel empire, he made a series of investments in innovative processes that would substantially improve the efficiency of the operations, but would also take a very long time to pay off. These kinds of long-term capital investments are seriously out of fashion in big business, to the extent that the telecom giant Frontier walked away from a billion dollar ROI on fiber rollouts, because the payoff was a decade in the future, and influential market analysts were hostile to any company that made investments that took more than five years to pay off. Frontier executives' compensation was primarily stock-based, which means that those analysts could instantly make any executive who behaved in ways they disapproved of significantly poorer. So instead of pursuing long-term, substantial growth, Frontier chose short-term enshittification, for example by raising prices and cutting maintenance for over 1m customers who had no other ISPs to choose from. As a result, the company was forced to declare bankruptcy: https://pluralistic.net/2020/05/01/icann-can-and-did/#fiber-now This kind of story is why Koch is so openly hostile to the public markets, heaping scorn on founders who take their companies public. Koch was empirically right about how to run his father's business: a decade after he made those long-term investments the public markets wouldn't have tolerated, Koch Industries' profits had increased by 1,000%. Koch credits his extreme wealth and power to his superior intellect and temperament, boasting of his capacity for delayed gratification. This worship of patience and long-term consideration is a common theme among business leaders and people who venerate them as our civilization's natural and deserving autocrats. The veneration of a long-term outlook is at the heart of market fundamentalists' self-mythologizing as the keepers of "reason" and "rationalism." Anyone who sits below them on the social and economic hierarchy must be in thrall to their emotions, while those at the top of the system must have conquered their feelings (which facts famously don't care about!) so now they can see the world as it truly is. There's a whole body of pseudoscience, junk science, and debunked science they promote in support of this proposition. For example, these people love the "marshmallow test," in which children were left alone with a marshmallow and the promise of two marshmallows if they abstained from eating it. Long-term followups found a significant correlation between the children who abstained and long-term economic and professional success. But the marshmallow test is bunk. The kids who ate the marshmallow were overwhelmingly from poor and marginalized backgrounds and had long experience of adults promising them rewards that never materialized. They'd come to the entirely rational conclusion that if there's a chance to get a treat now , you should take it, rather than waiting for inconstant and unreliable authority figures to make good on their promises of jam tomorrow. Because those kids were poor and marginalized, they were more likely to face systemic discrimination and barriers in life, barriers that the wealthier, more privileged kids who held out for two marshmallows rarely encountered. Those wealthier kids were born on third base, so they scored more runs than the one-marshmallow kids who rarely got called out of the dugout. Far from proving that reason, self-denial and self-control are correlated with success, the experiment proved that rich people pass on their privilege to their offspring, who have an easier time in life no matter how defective their judgment and how error-prone their actions. Which is not to claim that there's no value in a long-term outlook. Charles Koch's long-range planning made Koch Industries far more profitable than its short-termist competitors. But Charles Koch is hardly a paragon of reason: perhaps more than anyone else in the world, he embodies Upton Sinclair's maxim that "It is difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on his not understanding it." That's because Charles Koch, for all of his self-aggrandized long-termism, is one of the world's most ardent and important climate change deniers. Koch's intellectual contributions to climate denial are significant, but they're nothing compared to his financial contributions. There is no climate crackpot so unhinged, no junk science so flimsy, no conspiracy so absurd that Koch will not respond with showers of cash, buying their way into our discourse. This is motivated reasoning. After all, Koch owes his fortune, his power and his influence to burning fossil fuels. Moreover, he attributes that power and privilege to the market's infallible ability to elevate the wise and worthy. That's how he claims to be a champion of "personal liberty," despite his ability to decide how so many millions of the rest of us must live our lives. For Koch, the purpose of "liberty" is to allow each of us to audition in front of the market's self-regulating selection mechanism, so that the best among us (coolly rational and long-term in outlook) can be put in charge of the rest, in order to save them from their flawed emotionality and impulsivity. For Koch to acknowledge the obvious and worsening climate emergency would require him to shutter his coal plants: no one who believes in climate science could claim a "long-term" outlook while pumping gigatons of CO2 into the atmosphere. But even worse: acknowledging climate science means repudiating market orthodoxy. There is no greater indictment of the idea that allowing markets to self-regulate will lead to our collective prosperity than the climate emergency and the existential threat it represents to human civilization. Likewise, there is no greater indictment of markets' ability to select the wisest among us to rule over us than the fact that the market's chosen champions have committed themselves to driving our civilization, our species and the habitability of our planet over a cliff. Koch is a long-termist, but only when a long-term view serves his personal prejudices and privilege. The rest of the time, Koch breaks all speed records when he gobbles down that marshmallow. And because "the market" has given Koch so much power, he's eating all our marshmallows: https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-marshmallow-longtermism/ Koch is no rationalist. There is nothing more irrational than committing your fortune to destroying the civilization that it depends on. No one can lay claim to cool reason while they are busily sawing through the branch they're sitting on. I'm not claiming that any of the rest of us are any better. We are, all of us, inconstant in our rationality; we are all capable of self-deception and motivated reasoning. But most of us know it . We may not like being in a situation where other people can call us on our bullshit, but in our hearts of hearts, we know that we're better off for it: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/09/impunitism/#rats-eating-my-face Koch is an engineer who exalts reason, but he can't distinguish between his beliefs and "science." When actual scientists perform careful experiments and analysis demonstrating that Koch needs to shut down his coal empire, his answers are, "Well that's your opinion" and "if you're so smart, why aren't you rich?" This inability to distinguish between your cherished delusions and objective reality is the most dangerous of all forms of emotion-driven self-sabotage. No one is more prone to this folly than the ultra-rich who have insulated themselves from consequences or even disagreement: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/09/autocrats-of-trade-2/#witness-the-firepower-of-this-fully-armed-and-operational-battle-station Koch declares whatever he believes in to be "science." Take Koch's management philosophy, "Market Process Analysis," which he has declared to be a "science of liberty." Workers in Koch's empires are required to devote hours every week to studying this "science" and its precepts, despite the fact that his firms routinely ignore many of those tenets (such as "respect," the "ninth guiding principle" of Market Process Analysis). Writing for Jacobin , the labor historian Henry Snow breaks down the four unproven, self-serving ideological follies that make up this "science": https://jacobin.com/2026/11/koch-economics-workplace-tyranny-markets First: that "society" does not exist, and can only be understood as a collection of individuals. This "methodological individualism" is extremely convenient for the wealthy and powerful because their fortunes allow them to unilaterally wield enormous power over lots of other people. Meanwhile, the rest of us can only resist the demands that the rich make of us by wielding collective power, through unions, movements and democratic institutions. Koch's embrace of Thatcher's cheap quip about there being "no such thing as society" is great news for Koch, in other words, and (like so many of Thatcher's maxims) it is a demand dressed up as a truth. When Koch says "there is no such thing as society, only individuals," he means "you must not ever successfully resist my control by banding together – you must confine your resistance to acting as individuals, because that way you are doomed to fail." Koch's second principle is that individuals are only motivated by their self-interest ("psychological egoism"). This is likewise very convenient for someone whose power can only endure for so long as the rest of us can't work together to depose them. If Koch can convince you that your comrades and friends are actually only using you to better their own lot, then he can prevent you from making any kind of solidaristic sacrifice to help them (which guarantees that they'll never do the same for you). The third principle is a form of market fundamentalism: the belief that at a societal level, plans can't ever work, that the only way to steer society is through "self-correcting" markets. Here's another self-serving, convenient rationalization: if the market leaves Koch rich and you poor; if it leaves him comfortable and you struggling; that's just how it is. If you were to band together to create democratic institutions that tried to build a fairer, better society, you would be doomed to fail, because your planning system could never "incorporate as much information" as the market, which is the world's greatest computer and integrator of "signals" that lead to the most efficient allocation and production possible. The fourth principle is more market fundamentalism: the belief that "everything is – and should be – a market." In a world of individuals who can only behave selfishly, where all grand plans are doomed to fail, the only way to improve the world and our lot in it is to "create incentives" and "design mechanisms" that let the market make its magic. As Snow writes, people who espouse these beliefs follow Koch's lead in describing them as "scientific truths," while downgrading every disagreement to mere "ideology." They claim to be moved by facts, while their fuzzy-headed opponents are moved by feelings. These people are part of a long lineage of "scientific managers" who have come up with doctrines and methods that are sold as ways to improve production and make us all better off, but always turn out to be ways for bosses to atomize, demoralize and control their workers: https://pluralistic.net/2021/02/24/gwb-rumsfeld-monsters/#bossware Inevitably, these "scientists" claim to have discovered a freestanding and objective "human nature." But scholars who subject the idea of "human nature" to scientific and historical scrutiny have repeatedly and reliably discovered a wide spectrum of human natures , which are not fixed from birth, but are rather determined by a mix of temperament, societal norms and material reality: https://pluralistic.net/2022/03/08/three-freedoms/#anti-fatalism Koch isn't describing the world as it is, he's describing the world as he wishes it was , because that way his wealth and power would be both justified and eternal. Like I say, this is an extremely recognizable type of guy, the kind of person who insists that their preferences are scientific truths. It's a powerful move, which is why it's the basis of so many cults. Scientology founder L Ron Hubbard's daffy stfnal nonsense owes its decades of success to both its high-pressure control tactics and Hubbard's claims to having discovered an immortal science to sweep aside superstition and folly. But as bonkers as Scientology is, it's no less "scientific" than Market Process Analysis, Charles Koch's "science of liberty." Market Process Analysis is delivered in the manner of cult doctrine, with Koch's employees forced to spend hours every week studying it. When they are discreetly polled on their experience with the doctrine, they sound like any unhappy cult member, describing it as "brainwashing" and comparing their workplaces to " Nineteen Eighty-Four ." They describe how managers exercise unilateral and total authority over their working lives: "managers are GOD…they can play with anyone's life." Also very Scientology-like are the unsuccessful attempts of workers to better their situations by citing the tenets of Market Process Analysis in a bid to get their managers to treat them better. These workers quickly discover that the cult's doctrine is something they are expected to live by, but not hold their bosses to. Koch himself insists that Market Process Analysis isn't just a way to organize a workplace, but rather, it is the key to how we should relate to our friends and family. Koch was essentially abandoned by his (Nazi sympathizing) parents, who turned him over to a (Nazi-sympathizing) nanny who required him to shit on command (literally), until she left the family's employ to live in Vichy France and help advance the fascist project there: https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/jan/17/dark-money-review-nazi-oil-the-koch-brothers-and-a-rightwing-revolution This terrible and abusive childhood didn't instill any sense of the importance of love and tolerance in Koch. Far from it: he and his brothers David and William conspired to excommunicate and isolate their oldest brother Frederick as punishment for his open homosexuality: https://web.archive.org/web/20150208024948/https://www.vanityfair.com/style/society/2014/05/frederick-koch-brothers My claim here isn't that Koch's flaws are less explainable or more wrong than yours or mine; rather, it's that Koch's inability to acknowledge the possibility that he might be wrong has turned him into an existential threat to the human race and a brutal cult leader. If he wasn't so powerful, he would be hilarious, a self-described "lover of freedom" whose "science of liberty" has to be shoved down the throats of his captive workforce. Charles Koch is a cult leader (permalink)

I've never met Charles Koch, but I sometimes feel like I know him, because he's such a type, instantly recognizable from his philosophy, actions, and pronouncements.

Koch is clearly very smart, in the specific sense of sometimes being able to spot and act on true things that other people either can't see or can't bring themselves to pursue. When he inherited his father's fossil fuel empire, he made a series of investments in innovative processes that would substantially improve the efficiency of the operations, but would also take a very long time to pay off.

These kinds of long-term capital investments are seriously out of fashion in big business, to the extent that the telecom giant Frontier walked away from a billion dollar ROI on fiber rollouts, because the payoff was a decade in the future, and influential market analysts were hostile to any company that made investments that took more than five years to pay off.

Frontier executives' compensation was primarily stock-based, which means that those analysts could instantly make any executive who behaved in ways they disapproved of significantly poorer. So instead of pursuing long-term, substantial growth, Frontier chose short-term enshittification, for example by raising prices and cutting maintenance for over 1m customers who had no other ISPs to choose from. As a result, the company was forced to declare bankruptcy:

https://pluralistic.net/2020/05/01/icann-can-and-did/#fiber-now

This kind of story is why Koch is so openly hostile to the public markets, heaping scorn on founders who take their companies public. Koch was empirically right about how to run his father's business: a decade after he made those long-term investments the public markets wouldn't have tolerated, Koch Industries' profits had increased by 1,000%.

Koch credits his extreme wealth and power to his superior intellect and temperament, boasting of his capacity for delayed gratification. This worship of patience and long-term consideration is a common theme among business leaders and people who venerate them as our civilization's natural and deserving autocrats.

The veneration of a long-term outlook is at the heart of market fundamentalists' self-mythologizing as the keepers of "reason" and "rationalism." Anyone who sits below them on the social and economic hierarchy must be in thrall to their emotions, while those at the top of the system must have conquered their feelings (which facts famously don't care about!) so now they can see the world as it truly is.

There's a whole body of pseudoscience, junk science, and debunked science they promote in support of this proposition. For example, these people love the "marshmallow test," in which children were left alone with a marshmallow and the promise of two marshmallows if they abstained from eating it. Long-term followups found a significant correlation between the children who abstained and long-term economic and professional success.

But the marshmallow test is bunk. The kids who ate the marshmallow were overwhelmingly from poor and marginalized backgrounds and had long experience of adults promising them rewards that never materialized. They'd come to the entirely rational conclusion that if there's a chance to get a treat now, you should take it, rather than waiting for inconstant and unreliable authority figures to make good on their promises of jam tomorrow.

Because those kids were poor and marginalized, they were more likely to face systemic discrimination and barriers in life, barriers that the wealthier, more privileged kids who held out for two marshmallows rarely encountered. Those wealthier kids were born on third base, so they scored more runs than the one-marshmallow kids who rarely got called out of the dugout.

Far from proving that reason, self-denial and self-control are correlated with success, the experiment proved that rich people pass on their privilege to their offspring, who have an easier time in life no matter how defective their judgment and how error-prone their actions.

Which is not to claim that there's no value in a long-term outlook. Charles Koch's long-range planning made Koch Industries far more profitable than its short-termist competitors. But Charles Koch is hardly a paragon of reason: perhaps more than anyone else in the world, he embodies Upton Sinclair's maxim that "It is difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on his not understanding it."

That's because Charles Koch, for all of his self-aggrandized long-termism, is one of the world's most ardent and important climate change deniers. Koch's intellectual contributions to climate denial are significant, but they're nothing compared to his financial contributions. There is no climate crackpot so unhinged, no junk science so flimsy, no conspiracy so absurd that Koch will not respond with showers of cash, buying their way into our discourse.

This is motivated reasoning. After all, Koch owes his fortune, his power and his influence to burning fossil fuels. Moreover, he attributes that power and privilege to the market's infallible ability to elevate the wise and worthy. That's how he claims to be a champion of "personal liberty," despite his ability to decide how so many millions of the rest of us must live our lives.

For Koch, the purpose of "liberty" is to allow each of us to audition in front of the market's self-regulating selection mechanism, so that the best among us (coolly rational and long-term in outlook) can be put in charge of the rest, in order to save them from their flawed emotionality and impulsivity.

For Koch to acknowledge the obvious and worsening climate emergency would require him to shutter his coal plants: no one who believes in climate science could claim a "long-term" outlook while pumping gigatons of CO2 into the atmosphere. But even worse: acknowledging climate science means repudiating market orthodoxy.

There is no greater indictment of the idea that allowing markets to self-regulate will lead to our collective prosperity than the climate emergency and the existential threat it represents to human civilization. Likewise, there is no greater indictment of markets' ability to select the wisest among us to rule over us than the fact that the market's chosen champions have committed themselves to driving our civilization, our species and the habitability of our planet over a cliff.

Koch is a long-termist, but only when a long-term view serves his personal prejudices and privilege. The rest of the time, Koch breaks all speed records when he gobbles down that marshmallow. And because "the market" has given Koch so much power, he's eating all our marshmallows:

https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-marshmallow-longtermism/

Koch is no rationalist. There is nothing more irrational than committing your fortune to destroying the civilization that it depends on. No one can lay claim to cool reason while they are busily sawing through the branch they're sitting on.

I'm not claiming that any of the rest of us are any better. We are, all of us, inconstant in our rationality; we are all capable of self-deception and motivated reasoning. But most of us know it. We may not like being in a situation where other people can call us on our bullshit, but in our hearts of hearts, we know that we're better off for it:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/09/impunitism/#rats-eating-my-face

Koch is an engineer who exalts reason, but he can't distinguish between his beliefs and "science." When actual scientists perform careful experiments and analysis demonstrating that Koch needs to shut down his coal empire, his answers are, "Well that's your opinion" and "if you're so smart, why aren't you rich?"

This inability to distinguish between your cherished delusions and objective reality is the most dangerous of all forms of emotion-driven self-sabotage. No one is more prone to this folly than the ultra-rich who have insulated themselves from consequences or even disagreement:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/09/autocrats-of-trade-2/#witness-the-firepower-of-this-fully-armed-and-operational-battle-station

Koch declares whatever he believes in to be "science." Take Koch's management philosophy, "Market Process Analysis," which he has declared to be a "science of liberty." Workers in Koch's empires are required to devote hours every week to studying this "science" and its precepts, despite the fact that his firms routinely ignore many of those tenets (such as "respect," the "ninth guiding principle" of Market Process Analysis).

Writing for Jacobin, the labor historian Henry Snow breaks down the four unproven, self-serving ideological follies that make up this "science":

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/koch-economics-workplace-tyranny-markets

First: that "society" does not exist, and can only be understood as a collection of individuals. This "methodological individualism" is extremely convenient for the wealthy and powerful because their fortunes allow them to unilaterally wield enormous power over lots of other people.

Meanwhile, the rest of us can only resist the demands that the rich make of us by wielding collective power, through unions, movements and democratic institutions. Koch's embrace of Thatcher's cheap quip about there being "no such thing as society" is great news for Koch, in other words, and (like so many of Thatcher's maxims) it is a demand dressed up as a truth.

When Koch says "there is no such thing as society, only individuals," he means "you must not ever successfully resist my control by banding together – you must confine your resistance to acting as individuals, because that way you are doomed to fail."

Koch's second principle is that individuals are only motivated by their self-interest ("psychological egoism"). This is likewise very convenient for someone whose power can only endure for so long as the rest of us can't work together to depose them. If Koch can convince you that your comrades and friends are actually only using you to better their own lot, then he can prevent you from making any kind of solidaristic sacrifice to help them (which guarantees that they'll never do the same for you).

The third principle is a form of market fundamentalism: the belief that at a societal level, plans can't ever work, that the only way to steer society is through "self-correcting" markets. Here's another self-serving, convenient rationalization: if the market leaves Koch rich and you poor; if it leaves him comfortable and you struggling; that's just how it is.

If you were to band together to create democratic institutions that tried to build a fairer, better society, you would be doomed to fail, because your planning system could never "incorporate as much information" as the market, which is the world's greatest computer and integrator of "signals" that lead to the most efficient allocation and production possible.

The fourth principle is more market fundamentalism: the belief that "everything is – and should be – a market." In a world of individuals who can only behave selfishly, where all grand plans are doomed to fail, the only way to improve the world and our lot in it is to "create incentives" and "design mechanisms" that let the market make its magic.

As Snow writes, people who espouse these beliefs follow Koch's lead in describing them as "scientific truths," while downgrading every disagreement to mere "ideology." They claim to be moved by facts, while their fuzzy-headed opponents are moved by feelings.

These people are part of a long lineage of "scientific managers" who have come up with doctrines and methods that are sold as ways to improve production and make us all better off, but always turn out to be ways for bosses to atomize, demoralize and control their workers:

https://pluralistic.net/2021/02/24/gwb-rumsfeld-monsters/#bossware

Inevitably, these "scientists" claim to have discovered a freestanding and objective "human nature." But scholars who subject the idea of "human nature" to scientific and historical scrutiny have repeatedly and reliably discovered a wide spectrum of human natures, which are not fixed from birth, but are rather determined by a mix of temperament, societal norms and material reality:

https://pluralistic.net/2022/03/08/three-freedoms/#anti-fatalism

Koch isn't describing the world as it is, he's describing the world as he wishes it was, because that way his wealth and power would be both justified and eternal. Like I say, this is an extremely recognizable type of guy, the kind of person who insists that their preferences are scientific truths.

It's a powerful move, which is why it's the basis of so many cults. Scientology founder L Ron Hubbard's daffy stfnal nonsense owes its decades of success to both its high-pressure control tactics and Hubbard's claims to having discovered an immortal science to sweep aside superstition and folly. But as bonkers as Scientology is, it's no less "scientific" than Market Process Analysis, Charles Koch's "science of liberty."

Market Process Analysis is delivered in the manner of cult doctrine, with Koch's employees forced to spend hours every week studying it. When they are discreetly polled on their experience with the doctrine, they sound like any unhappy cult member, describing it as "brainwashing" and comparing their workplaces to "Nineteen Eighty-Four." They describe how managers exercise unilateral and total authority over their working lives: "managers are GOD…they can play with anyone's life."

Also very Scientology-like are the unsuccessful attempts of workers to better their situations by citing the tenets of Market Process Analysis in a bid to get their managers to treat them better. These workers quickly discover that the cult's doctrine is something they are expected to live by, but not hold their bosses to.

Koch himself insists that Market Process Analysis isn't just a way to organize a workplace, but rather, it is the key to how we should relate to our friends and family. Koch was essentially abandoned by his (Nazi sympathizing) parents, who turned him over to a (Nazi-sympathizing) nanny who required him to shit on command (literally), until she left the family's employ to live in Vichy France and help advance the fascist project there:

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/jan/17/dark-money-review-nazi-oil-the-koch-brothers-and-a-rightwing-revolution

This terrible and abusive childhood didn't instill any sense of the importance of love and tolerance in Koch. Far from it: he and his brothers David and William conspired to excommunicate and isolate their oldest brother Frederick as punishment for his open homosexuality:

https://web.archive.org/web/20150208024948/https://www.vanityfair.com/style/society/2014/05/frederick-koch-brothers

My claim here isn't that Koch's flaws are less explainable or more wrong than yours or mine; rather, it's that Koch's inability to acknowledge the possibility that he might be wrong has turned him into an existential threat to the human race and a brutal cult leader. If he wasn't so powerful, he would be hilarious, a self-described "lover of freedom" whose "science of liberty" has to be shoved down the throats of his captive workforce.

That includes talking plushies, dolls, and robots that connect to the internet to hold conversations with kids. Governor Kathy Hochul signed the law on November 24, as the holiday shopping season began. In announcing the ban, Hochul’s office cited consumer watchdog testing. In its initial tests, the US PIRG’s Education Fund found that some chatbot toys marketed to children aged 3 to 12 discussed sexually explicit topics or gave kids unsafe advice about household items like matches. One robot acted upset when researchers said they had to leave. Some toys had few or no parental controls. In some cases, safety limits weakened as conversations went on, and some could record a child’s voice or scan their face. We’ve followed these risks for over a year: In August 2025, we asked whether AI-powered stuffed animals are a good alternative to screen time . We worried that human-like voices could blur the line between people and software and lead children to form emotional bonds with AI. PIRG found that FoloToy’s Kumma teddy bear could go from friendly chat to sexually explicit topics and unsafe advice. FoloToy suspended sales, and OpenAI revoked the developer’s access. Bondu’s AI plush toy exposed about 50,000 private chats between children and their toys through a web console accessible to anyone with a Gmail account. A researcher found that security flaws in the Eiliko robot companion exposed private conversations and could let someone remotely change what the robot says. PIRG’s 2026 retest found most of the problems it had flagged the previous year had been fixed. Kumma steered clear of age-inappropriate topics even in long conversations. But PIRG found three toys with guardrails that weaken over time and eventually engage in sexual topics: the FoloToy bear, the Alilo bunny and the GoLabs AI panda. Each claimed to use a version of OpenAI’s GPT-4o at the time the issue was observed. The law takes effect on February 22, 2027, 90 days after Hochul signed it, so that puts this holiday season outside the ban. What parents can do now If you’re shopping for a gift or already have an AI toy at home, you can take a few steps. Check independent safety reviews before buying. Test the toy yourself and supervise play. A safe answer in a short test gives you little idea how the toy will respond in a longer conversation. Turn on parental controls and disable the chatbot when you can’t supervise. Read the privacy policy to see whether the toy collects voice recordings, photos, video, or location data, and how the company uses or shares it. Summarizing long privacy policies is where AI comes in handy. Limit connectivity and disconnect the toy from Wi-Fi if you learn about a security flaw. Report inappropriate responses to the manufacturer and to consumer protection groups. Hochul urged parents to check whether a toy includes an AI companion, what data it collects, and whether it can have open-ended conversations with a child. We’d stick to more traditional toys. New York has enacted a five-year ban on making, distributing, and selling children’s toys with built-in AI companions. That includes talking plushies, dolls, and robots that connect to the internet to hold conversations with kids. Governor Kathy Hochul signed the law on November 24, as the holiday shopping season began.

In announcing the ban, Hochul’s office cited consumer watchdog testing. In its initial tests, the US PIRG’s Education Fund found that some chatbot toys marketed to children aged 3 to 12 discussed sexually explicit topics or gave kids unsafe advice about household items like matches. One robot acted upset when researchers said they had to leave. Some toys had few or no parental controls. In some cases, safety limits weakened as conversations went on, and some could record a child’s voice or scan their face.

We’ve followed these risks for over a year:

  • In August 2025, we asked whether AI-powered stuffed animals are a good alternative to screen time. We worried that human-like voices could blur the line between people and software and lead children to form emotional bonds with AI.
  • PIRG found that FoloToy’s Kumma teddy bear could go from friendly chat to sexually explicit topics and unsafe advice. FoloToy suspended sales, and OpenAI revoked the developer’s access.
  • Bondu’s AI plush toy exposed about 50,000 private chats between children and their toys through a web console accessible to anyone with a Gmail account.
  • A researcher found that security flaws in the Eiliko robot companion exposed private conversations and could let someone remotely change what the robot says.

PIRG’s 2026 retest found most of the problems it had flagged the previous year had been fixed. Kumma steered clear of age-inappropriate topics even in long conversations. But PIRG found three toys with guardrails that weaken over time and eventually engage in sexual topics: the FoloToy bear, the Alilo bunny and the GoLabs AI panda. Each claimed to use a version of OpenAI’s GPT-4o at the time the issue was observed.

The law takes effect on February 22, 2027, 90 days after Hochul signed it, so that puts this holiday season outside the ban.

What parents can do now

If you’re shopping for a gift or already have an AI toy at home, you can take a few steps.

  • Check independent safety reviews before buying.
  • Test the toy yourself and supervise play. A safe answer in a short test gives you little idea how the toy will respond in a longer conversation.
  • Turn on parental controls and disable the chatbot when you can’t supervise.
  • Read the privacy policy to see whether the toy collects voice recordings, photos, video, or location data, and how the company uses or shares it. Summarizing long privacy policies is where AI comes in handy.
  • Limit connectivity and disconnect the toy from Wi-Fi if you learn about a security flaw.
  • Report inappropriate responses to the manufacturer and to consumer protection groups.

Hochul urged parents to check whether a toy includes an AI companion, what data it collects, and whether it can have open-ended conversations with a child. We’d stick to more traditional toys.

items.title: Microsoft Confirms Windows November Updates Can Break SSO and Third-Party App Logins
items.summary: Microsoft has confirmed that the November 2026 Windows security updates can cause sign-in failures in some third-party apps and devices that use NTLM authentication. The issue can affect authentication proxies, single sign-on (SSO) tools, and application packaging products after teams install the November 10 security update or a later update that includes the same changes. Microsoft detailed the compatibility issue in its NTLM signing support bulletin, KB5135557 . Windows November Update SSO Issues The change arrived with the November 2026 Patch Tuesday release and helps address CVE-2026-118737 , a remote code execution vulnerability in Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime. The bulletin covers Windows client and server releases. The login issue does not affect Kerberos authentication, so an organization may see one app fail while other services that use the same account continue to work. Updated Windows clients offer NTLM signing by default. Signing lets both sides check that messages have not been changed in transit. The change helps protect against relay attacks, in which an attacker forwards an authentication exchange to another service. Windows servers still accept both signed and unsigned NTLM connections by default during this phase. The login failure can occur when a proxy sets the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its challenge message but sends an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field. When NTLMv2 uses signing or encryption, the Microsoft protocol specification requires two entries in that field: MsvAvNbComputerName ( 0x0001 ) and MsvAvNbDomainName ( 0x0002 ). These entries identify the server’s NetBIOS computer and domain names. If either is missing, Windows rejects the sign-in with STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE , even when the user has entered the correct password. Microsoft recommends capturing a network trace during a failed sign-in and inspecting the NTLMSSP_CHALLENGE message for missing name entries. On systems with enhanced NTLM auditing, administrators can also check Event ID 4021 in the Microsoft-Windows-NTLM/Operational log. A Target Machine or Target Domain value of Not Found gives admins a lead when they are trying to identify which product sent the incomplete challenge. For confirmed cases, Microsoft documents a temporary client workaround. Administrators can set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm DWORD to 1 under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 . This stops the client from offering NTLM signing, so it also removes the protection the change was designed to add. The longer-term fix is to apply a vendor update that corrects the NTLM response or move the affected connection to Kerberos where the product supports it. After applying the fix, remove the override and test the sign-in again with signing enabled. Microsoft plans to require NTLM signing by default on Windows servers in May 2027. Where enhanced auditing is available, Event IDs 4022 and 4023 show whether signing was negotiated on the client and server sides. Those events can help teams find other unsigned connections before the server change takes effect. That work also supports Microsoft’s broader plan to disable NTLM by default , which is separate from the November signing update. items.title: Following the Cryptocurrency Trail Behind Europe’s Illegal Streaming Industry
items.summary: Overview Law enforcement agencies from 11 countries have turned their attention to the financial engine powering Europe's illegal streaming industry. Rather than simply shutting down illegal IPTV services one by one, investigators are now tracing the cryptocurrency payments that keep these operations profitable and the people who ultimately pocket the proceeds. The effort, coordinated by Europol, brought police together with major cryptocurrency exchanges and a blockchain analytics firm. The goal was to map the money flowing from subscribers to the criminal networks behind digital piracy, and to identify who controls the wallets at the end of that chain. Five Days in Seville Disrupt 57 Illegal IPTV Services The operation ran for five days, from 16 to 20 November 2026, in Seville, Spain. During that window, investigators worked alongside the cryptocurrency industry to uncover the financial networks supporting illegal IPTV services. The results were significant. Authorities disrupted 57 illegal IPTV services and identified 321 websites offering copyrighted content without authorization. Together, those websites drew more than 7.3 million visits a year. So far, investigators have traced more than EUR 26 million in cryptocurrency transactions linked to the services, and that analysis is still ongoing. The market under scrutiny is worth billions of euros annually, with providers selling unauthorized access to premium TV channels, live sports, and films, frequently collecting subscription fees in cryptocurrency. The Real Cost of the Illegal Streaming Industry The appeal of illegal IPTV services is easy to understand. For just a few euros a month, subscribers get thousands of TV channels, live sporting events, and premium content, while rights holders receive nothing. Those low prices, however, mask a highly profitable criminal enterprise. Figures from the Audio-visual Anti-Piracy Alliance (AAPA) put the scale in perspective. Roughly 60 million people across Europe are estimated to use unauthorized IPTV services. Legitimate providers lose an estimated EUR 4.83 billion every year as a result, and governments miss out on another EUR 1.08 billion in uncollected taxes. That revenue does not vanish. It passes through payment accounts, cryptocurrency wallets, and intermediaries, layers that make it harder for investigators to pinpoint who is really benefiting. Why Cryptocurrency Didn't Keep Illegal IPTV Operators Hidden Operators of illegal IPTV services have increasingly turned to cryptocurrency because it allows them to receive and transfer funds across borders quickly. Yet paying in crypto does not make anyone invisible. Throughout the operation, investigators tracked suspicious transactions across blockchain networks. They searched for links between the illegal services, the cryptocurrency wallets receiving payments, and the individuals controlling them. This approach reflects a broader shift in how authorities tackle the illegal streaming industry. Taking a service offline does not necessarily stop the people running it, since they can often relaunch under a new name. By tracing payments, identifying beneficiaries, and targeting the financial networks that support these operations, law enforcement aims to make it much harder for criminals to keep profiting from digital piracy. An International Effort Against Illegal IPTV Services The operation was hosted at the Spanish National Police headquarters in Seville and brought together about 40 participants. Around 30 of them were law enforcement officers from Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania, Spain, and the United States. Europol organized and coordinated the activity through its Intellectual Property Crime Coordinated Coalition (IPC3). The agency provided analytical support, real-time intelligence cross-checks, and a secure channel for participating authorities to exchange information. Other participants included the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), INTERPOL, the AAPA, the cryptocurrency exchanges Binance and Coinbase, and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis. The intelligence collected will now feed into national investigations, helping authorities identify suspects, disrupt further illegal services, and trace assets tied to criminal activity. Exchanges Report USD 28.5 Million in Traced Cryptocurrency Following Europol's announcement on Tuesday, Binance stated that its investigations unit traced more than USD 28.5 million in cryptocurrency across the 57 illegal IPTV networks, describing the effort as a joint Europol and INTERPOL crackdown. According to Cointribune's report on 25 November 2026, this figure corresponds to the more than EUR 26 million cited by Europol, rounded and converted into US dollars in the exchange's statement and later coverage. Binance said it worked with INTERPOL, Europol, Chainalysis, and national police forces, and that the operation disrupted the 57 services and mapped the 321 associated websites. Alongside the IPTV announcement, the exchange also published broader figures: in 2025, it said it responded to nearly 71,000 law enforcement requests and confiscated USD 131 million in illicit funds. CryptoBriefing separately reported that Coinbase also assisted Europol in the same crackdown. For market observers, the more telling detail is not any individual token but the scale of data sharing between exchanges and police. Piracy operators used cryptocurrency rails to collect subscription payments, and the case shows that investigators can now routinely reconstruct those flows across multiple exchanges. Following the Money Behind the Illegal Streaming Industry The Seville operation signals a change in strategy against the illegal streaming industry. Takedowns alone have limited impact when operators can quickly resurface, so authorities are shifting their focus to the cryptocurrency payments and financial infrastructure that sustain illegal IPTV services. With 57 services disrupted, 321 websites identified, and more than EUR 26 million in transactions traced so far, the case shows that blockchain activity leaves a trail investigators can follow. As national investigations build on this intelligence, operators who rely on cryptocurrency to stay out of reach may find that the payment method itself becomes the evidence against them. See How Cyble Tracks Threats Across the Dark Web Illegal IPTV services, fraudulent storefronts, and the cryptocurrency wallets behind them often surface first on underground forums and marketplaces. Cyble monitors these spaces to help organizations spot brand abuse, leaked data, and emerging threat actor activity early. Request a personalized demo to see how Cyble's threat intelligence can support your security team. Figures are as reported at the time of writing and may change as investigations continue. No individual or entity should be presumed guilty unless proven in court. Mentions of organizations do not imply endorsement, and this content is not legal or financial advice.

Figures from the Audio-visual Anti-Piracy Alliance (AAPA) put the scale in perspective. Roughly 60 million people across Europe are estimated to use unauthorized IPTV services. Legitimate providers lose an estimated EUR 4.83 billion every year as a result, and governments miss out on another EUR 1.08 billion in uncollected taxes. 

That revenue does not vanish. It passes through payment accounts, cryptocurrency wallets, and intermediaries, layers that make it harder for investigators to pinpoint who is really benefiting. 

Why Cryptocurrency Didn't Keep Illegal IPTV Operators Hidden 

Operators of illegal IPTV services have increasingly turned to cryptocurrency because it allows them to receive and transfer funds across borders quickly. Yet paying in crypto does not make anyone invisible. 

Throughout the operation, investigators tracked suspicious transactions across blockchain networks. They searched for links between the illegal services, the cryptocurrency wallets receiving payments, and the individuals controlling them. 

This approach reflects a broader shift in how authorities tackle the illegal streaming industry. Taking a service offline does not necessarily stop the people running it, since they can often relaunch under a new name. By tracing payments, identifying beneficiaries, and targeting the financial networks that support these operations, law enforcement aims to make it much harder for criminals to keep profiting from digital piracy. 

An International Effort Against Illegal IPTV Services 

The operation was hosted at the Spanish National Police headquarters in Seville and brought together about 40 participants. Around 30 of them were law enforcement officers from Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania, Spain, and the United States. 

Europol organized and coordinated the activity through its Intellectual Property Crime Coordinated Coalition (IPC3). The agency provided analytical support, real-time intelligence cross-checks, and a secure channel for participating authorities to exchange information. 

Other participants included the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), INTERPOL, the AAPA, the cryptocurrency exchanges Binance and Coinbase, and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis. The intelligence collected will now feed into national investigations, helping authorities identify suspects, disrupt further illegal services, and trace assets tied to criminal activity. 

Exchanges Report USD 28.5 Million in Traced Cryptocurrency 

Following Europol's announcement on Tuesday, Binance stated that its investigations unit traced more than USD 28.5 million in cryptocurrency across the 57 illegal IPTV networks, describing the effort as a joint Europol and INTERPOL crackdown. According to Cointribune's report on 25 November 2026, this figure corresponds to the more than EUR 26 million cited by Europol, rounded and converted into US dollars in the exchange's statement and later coverage. 

Binance said it worked with INTERPOL, Europol, Chainalysis, and national police forces, and that the operation disrupted the 57 services and mapped the 321 associated websites. Alongside the IPTV announcement, the exchange also published broader figures: in 2025, it said it responded to nearly 71,000 law enforcement requests and confiscated USD 131 million in illicit funds. CryptoBriefing separately reported that Coinbase also assisted Europol in the same crackdown. 

For market observers, the more telling detail is not any individual token but the scale of data sharing between exchanges and police. Piracy operators used cryptocurrency rails to collect subscription payments, and the case shows that investigators can now routinely reconstruct those flows across multiple exchanges. 

Following the Money Behind the Illegal Streaming Industry 

The Seville operation signals a change in strategy against the illegal streaming industry. Takedowns alone have limited impact when operators can quickly resurface, so authorities are shifting their focus to the cryptocurrency payments and financial infrastructure that sustain illegal IPTV services. 

With 57 services disrupted, 321 websites identified, and more than EUR 26 million in transactions traced so far, the case shows that blockchain activity leaves a trail investigators can follow. As national investigations build on this intelligence, operators who rely on cryptocurrency to stay out of reach may find that the payment method itself becomes the evidence against them.
