items.title: Drupal Warns of Active Attacks Exploiting New Critical Website Takeover Vulnerability
items.summary: Drupal has warned that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-136716, a highly critical access bypass that can let them take over vulnerable websites without signing in. The Drupal Security Team confirmed the attacks in its November 25 security advisory and released updates for three supported Drupal core branches. The team did not say how many sites had been compromised. The flaw affects the installer that ships with Drupal core. Sites that had already secured the installer are not vulnerable, Drupal says. But some sites in unusual or incomplete installation states, including live production sites, remained exposed even after applying the previous installer fixes. Drupal rated the flaw 21 out of 25. A successful attack can expose private site data and let attackers change or delete it. Drupal Website Takeover Flaw Drupal’s November 18 security advisory addressed several installer flaws, including a separate remote code execution vulnerability, CVE-2026-132165. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of the earlier Drupal installer attacks , attackers were already targeting live sites. The November 25 advisory covers a different flaw that leaves some sites open to takeover despite the earlier fixes. That distinction also matters when reading Cyber Security News’ coverage of CISA’s Drupal exploitation warning . The Drupal flaw flagged by CISA was CVE-2026-132165, not the new access bypass. Drupal says the admin interface does not show whether a site is in the affected state. A site that was already compromised may no longer be in that state, so a dashboard that looks normal does not rule out a past break-in. Administrators should update Drupal 11.4.x to 11.4.14 , Drupal 11.3.x to 11.3.23 , and Drupal 10.6.x to 10.6.23 . Drupal 11.2.x and earlier 11.x releases, along with Drupal 10.5.x and earlier 10.x releases, no longer receive security coverage and should move to a supported branch. After installing the new release, run update.php . Drupal says this step is required to fix existing production sites in the affected state. Installing the new files alone is not enough. Follow Drupal’s guide to securing the installer to block public access to install.php after setup. Check that the installer is blocked without blocking update.php , which is a separate script. Sites using Drupal Steward’s recommended protections are covered against known attack methods, but Drupal still advises upgrading in case others are discovered. If the installer stayed reachable after the earlier advisory, review site logs for unauthorized access. Pay close attention to unexpected changes to Drupal’s user 1 account or actions taken by that account. Confirm you control its email address, and consider resetting its password. If you find signs of a break-in, follow Drupal’s guide for compromised sites and preserve a copy of the site files and database for investigation. Patching closes the flaw, but it does not undo changes an attacker made before the update. items.title: Exposed Hacker Servers Reveal U.S. Hospital Credentials, Corporate Cloud Access and Law Firm Targets
items.summary: Three exposed web directories revealed an intrusion crew’s collection of U.S. hospital credential records, a listing of more than 155,000 files and other objects in a manufacturer’s cloud storage, and a map of remote-access systems used by U.S. law firms. The recovered files showed that the operators had already used a valid cloud token. They did not show that the crew had breached a law firm or federal agency. The directories yielded 2,115 files with 1,981 distinct hashes, including scan results, attack logs, and copies of malware. Two directories shared an IP address; the third was on a separate host whose relationship to the first remains unresolved. The findings add to cases in which exposed attacker infrastructure reveals what criminals tried and, just as importantly, which attempts worked. Analysts from Hunt.io identified a malicious Java database driver, an Apollo-derived Windows payload, and a Poseidon-derived Linux implant in the recovered files. Their November 25 investigation separated what the malware could do from what the operators’ logs showed. Hunt.io said it notified the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency before publication so the agency could coordinate with affected organizations. Exposed Hacker Servers Reveal U.S. Hospital Credentials The hospital material included 8,460 unique email addresses, a separate dump of 3,570 authentication records, and a capture of a web server’s PHP configuration. Of the addresses, 6,929 belonged to the hospital system’s primary domain and 513 to an affiliated academic medical domain. Researchers could not establish how the authentication records were obtained or whether they still worked. A separate log recorded a hospital VPN session, but the files did not tie that session to the credential dump or show that patient data was taken. The manufacturer’s records provided clearer evidence of unauthorized access. The crew used a valid Azure shared access signature (SAS) token, which grants defined permissions to a storage resource, to list 155,568 objects. The names included a QuickBooks company file. The records show why stolen cloud access credentials matter even when attackers never open a file: a directory listing can expose what a company stores and how it organizes that data. The recovered output did not show file contents being downloaded. Crew’s open directories (Source – Hunt.io) In the legal sector, a target list held 563 unique entries, while scan results showed live VPNs, Citrix gateways, and client portals at more than 60 named firms. Those figures measure different things: the first counts list entries; the second reflects firms with services observed in scan results. Neither counts breaches. Separate reporting on VPN targeting explains why these internet-facing gateways draw attention, but Hunt.io’s evidence does not establish a ransomware link in this case. One firm, Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, faced more than scanning. The crew tested roughly 100 staff email and password pairs from a third-party leak against two Citrix gateways. The logs illustrate how credential stuffing works and why the result matters: the gateways rejected the credentials, and no VPN session was recorded. The wider sweep also reached the Small Business Administration, National Science Foundation, and other federal agencies, without evidence of successful access. Malicious Java Driver and What Defenders Should Check The Java archive posed as a database driver and could run code when a compatible application loaded it. A saved log recorded a launcher starting the Apollo-derived Windows executable, but did not prove that the payload connected back to the operators. The Linux file’s build metadata linked it to Poseidon, another agent associated with the Mythic command-and-control framework. Hunt.io did not verify that the Linux implant ran on a victim machine. The investigation also found AI coding tools in the operators’ environment and scripts that indexed Claude and OpenAI Codex credential files on other systems. That shows the crew was looking beyond browser passwords and cookies, but it does not establish that the operators obtained usable AI credentials or used an AI agent to carry out any specific intrusion. For defenders, the records suggest three places to look: VPN authentication logs for failed attempts followed by an unexpected session, Azure storage logs for unusual listing or read activity, and Java application inventories for unexpected database driver archives. Review token permissions and revoke or rotate a suspected exposed token as appropriate. Treat infrastructure matches as leads to verify, not proof of compromise: IP addresses can change hands, and a port number alone does not identify malicious traffic. items.title: Athar: a standard for service fingerprints
items.summary: Describe a service once, then convert it for every search engine and scanner. Gameel Ali, who works with me on Athar, recently shared queries on LinkedIn for finding ARTEX instances. ARTEX is the web console of an AI-driven, autonomous penetration-testing framework. It is deployed under many brand names: ARTEX, AntiFox, NKW, SHRIKE and others. I asked him how to run the same hunt on another platform. He replied with the query for that platform. Same hunt, different syntax. This is one title search for ARTEX on three engines: FOFA title="自主渗透测试控制台" Shodan http.title:"自主渗透测试控制台" Censys host.services.endpoints.http.html_title=~".*自主渗透测试控制台" So I asked: can’t we describe the fingerprint of these services once, in a generic format, and convert it into the queries of the different online services? A few hours later came the next idea. If a rule can become a search query, it can also become a Nuclei template or an Nmap NSE script. Then scanners can use the same fingerprints, not only search engines. That is Athar. Athar at a glance: a rule on the left, the athar CLI on the right. I’ve seen this problem before Nine years ago Thomas Patzke and I started Sigma for the same reason. Every SIEM had its own query language, and every detection idea was rewritten by hand for each of them. Sigma describes a log signature once, in YAML, and converters turn it into the query language of the SIEM you use. Today others carry the standard, and I’m more of an advisor: Thomas, Nasreddine Bencherchali, François Hubaut, Christian Burkard and Swachchhanda Shrawan Poudel do most of the work. Service fingerprints have the same problem today. A hunt gets published three or four times, once per search engine, as hand-written query strings. Those strings drift apart. They break when an engine changes its syntax; Censys deprecated its Legacy Search in September 2026. And nobody can test them. The principle is simple: describe a service once in a generic form, then convert it into the specific form each tool or service needs. It made sense for log signatures then. I think it makes sense for service fingerprints now. Describe a service once . Convert it for every engine and scanner. A rule If you can read a Sigma rule, you can read an Athar rule. The metadata and the detection block are Sigma. New are target, identifies, confidence and tests. title: Agentic Offensive Framework - ARTEX family target: protocol: http detection: selection: http.title|contains: 'Autonomous Penetration Testing Console' condition: selection identifies: family: artex category: offensive-tool confidence: high tests: - name: ARTEX console response: http.title: 'ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console' expect: match - name: Pentest vendor page response: http.title: 'Penetration Testing Services | Example Corp' expect: no_match Every brand of the console keeps the phrase “Autonomous Penetration Testing Console” in its title, so one condition finds all the rebrands. The real rule also matches the Chinese and Korean titles and reads the brand name out of the title. Two things matter here. A rule describes properties of a response, never engine syntax. Engine syntax lives in the converters, so when an engine changes its query language, we fix one converter, not every rule. And every rule carries tests: a response it must match and a near miss it must not. athar verify runs them, and CI rejects a rule whose tests fail. The athar CLI athar is a single Go binary. The rules are the only thing its commands share. athar convert turns rules into queries for FOFA, Shodan, Censys, ZoomEye, Modat Magnify and urlscan.io. Engines differ in what they can express, so every query carries a label. exact means the same results as the rule on that engine's data. approximate means the same intent with a looser operator, for example a whole-word match. superset means the engine can't express part of the rule, so the query drops that part and can only return more hosts, never fewer. Notes say what was lost and why. athar convert on two ARTEX rules: one query per engine, each with its label and notes. The same command writes Nuclei templates and an Nmap NSE script, so you can run the rules in the scanner you already use. Nuclei running converted Athar templates against local services that answer like an ARTEX console, an NKW rebrand, PentAGI and a Strix viewer. athar scan probes hosts you own or are allowed to test. Give it rules, hosts or CIDR ranges, and ports. It collects the TLS certificate, the response to GET /, the favicon and the banner, and prints one line per service that matches a rule: what it is, the brand it extracted, how confident the rule is, and the rule's author. athar scan -r rules/ -p 80,443,8787 10.0.0.0/24 athar scan on two live consoles on 25 November 2026: an ARTEX console, and an ARGOS rebrand that the family rule finds by its title. athar match is planned, not built yet. It will run rules over data you already have, such as engine exports or stored responses, without sending a packet. Its main job is to remove the over-matches of approximate queries: run a loose query on an engine, filter the export with athar match, and keep only what the rule really describes. Behind all three is one idea: the scanner defines what a rule means, not the engine query. scan and match use the same evaluator, so a query can be loose without making the results wrong. Have a look The first use case is the infrastructure of agentic offensive frameworks like ARTEX: AI-driven pentest consoles that keep changing their names. The format isn’t limited to them. C2 panels, phishing kits, appliances and ordinary server software fit the same way. Athar is a community project and a draft standard, so the rule format can still change. The rules are licensed under the Detection Rule License 1.1, the licence of the Sigma rules. The slide deck walks through the problem, a rule, the CLI and a real ARTEX hunt. Slide deck: the problem, a rule, the CLI and a real hunt for the ARTEX family. https://www.figma.com/deck/tFRGgSho2sEiq8mjW9pif8 Repository: https://github.com/Athar-HQ/Athar Latest release: binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows. https://github.com/Athar-HQ/Athar/releases/latest If you hunt infrastructure, send us your hunts as rules. You don’t have to write the YAML by hand: give your query and one host it found to an AI coding agent in the repository, and AGENTS.md tells it how to turn the query into a tested rule. And if something is missing, open an issue.

Describe a service once, then convert it for every search engine and scanner.

Gameel Ali, who works with me on Athar, recently shared queries on LinkedIn for finding ARTEX instances. ARTEX is the web console of an AI-driven, autonomous penetration-testing framework. It is deployed under many brand names: ARTEX, AntiFox, NKW, SHRIKE and others.

I asked him how to run the same hunt on another platform. He replied with the query for that platform. Same hunt, different syntax. This is one title search for ARTEX on three engines:

FOFA     title="自主渗透测试控制台"
Shodan   http.title:"自主渗透测试控制台"
Censys   host.services.endpoints.http.html_title=~".*自主渗透测试控制台"

So I asked: can’t we describe the fingerprint of these services once, in a generic format, and convert it into the queries of the different online services?

A few hours later came the next idea. If a rule can become a search query, it can also become a Nuclei template or an Nmap NSE script. Then scanners can use the same fingerprints, not only search engines.

That is Athar.

Athar at a glance: a rule on the left, the athar CLI on the right.I’ve seen this problem before

Nine years ago Thomas Patzke and I started Sigma for the same reason. Every SIEM had its own query language, and every detection idea was rewritten by hand for each of them. Sigma describes a log signature once, in YAML, and converters turn it into the query language of the SIEM you use. Today others carry the standard, and I’m more of an advisor: Thomas, Nasreddine Bencherchali, François Hubaut, Christian Burkard and Swachchhanda Shrawan Poudel do most of the work.

Service fingerprints have the same problem today. A hunt gets published three or four times, once per search engine, as hand-written query strings. Those strings drift apart. They break when an engine changes its syntax; Censys deprecated its Legacy Search in September 2026. And nobody can test them.

The principle is simple: describe a service once in a generic form, then convert it into the specific form each tool or service needs. It made sense for log signatures then. I think it makes sense for service fingerprints now.

Describe a service once. Convert it for every engine and scanner.A rule

If you can read a Sigma rule, you can read an Athar rule. The metadata and the detection block are Sigma. New are target, identifies, confidence and tests.

title: Agentic Offensive Framework - ARTEX family
target:
  protocol: http
detection:
  selection:
    http.title|contains: 'Autonomous Penetration Testing Console'
  condition: selection
identifies:
  family: artex
  category: offensive-tool
confidence: high
tests:
  - name: ARTEX console
    response:
      http.title: 'ARTEX — Autonomous Penetration Testing Console'
    expect: match
  - name: Pentest vendor page
    response:
      http.title: 'Penetration Testing Services | Example Corp'
    expect: no_match

Every brand of the console keeps the phrase “Autonomous Penetration Testing Console” in its title, so one condition finds all the rebrands. The real rule also matches the Chinese and Korean titles and reads the brand name out of the title.

Two things matter here. A rule describes properties of a response, never engine syntax. Engine syntax lives in the converters, so when an engine changes its query language, we fix one converter, not every rule. And every rule carries tests: a response it must match and a near miss it must not. athar verify runs them, and CI rejects a rule whose tests fail.

The athar CLI

athar is a single Go binary. The rules are the only thing its commands share.

athar convert turns rules into queries for FOFA, Shodan, Censys, ZoomEye, Modat Magnify and urlscan.io. Engines differ in what they can express, so every query carries a label. exact means the same results as the rule on that engine's data. approximate means the same intent with a looser operator, for example a whole-word match. superset means the engine can't express part of the rule, so the query drops that part and can only return more hosts, never fewer. Notes say what was lost and why.

athar convert on two ARTEX rules: one query per engine, each with its label and notes.

The same command writes Nuclei templates and an Nmap NSE script, so you can run the rules in the scanner you already use.

Nuclei running converted Athar templates against local services that answer like an ARTEX console, an NKW rebrand, PentAGI and a Strix viewer.

athar scan probes hosts you own or are allowed to test. Give it rules, hosts or CIDR ranges, and ports. It collects the TLS certificate, the response to GET /, the favicon and the banner, and prints one line per service that matches a rule: what it is, the brand it extracted, how confident the rule is, and the rule's author.

athar scan -r rules/ -p 80,443,8787 10.0.0.0/24
athar scan on two live consoles on 25 November 2026: an ARTEX console, and an ARGOS rebrand that the family rule finds by its title.

athar match is planned, not built yet. It will run rules over data you already have, such as engine exports or stored responses, without sending a packet. Its main job is to remove the over-matches of approximate queries: run a loose query on an engine, filter the export with athar match, and keep only what the rule really describes.

Behind all three is one idea: the scanner defines what a rule means, not the engine query. scan and match use the same evaluator, so a query can be loose without making the results wrong.

Have a look

The first use case is the infrastructure of agentic offensive frameworks like ARTEX: AI-driven pentest consoles that keep changing their names. The format isn’t limited to them. C2 panels, phishing kits, appliances and ordinary server software fit the same way.

Athar is a community project and a draft standard, so the rule format can still change. The rules are licensed under the Detection Rule License 1.1, the licence of the Sigma rules.

The slide deck walks through the problem, a rule, the CLI and a real ARTEX hunt.
  • Slide deck: the problem, a rule, the CLI and a real hunt for the ARTEX family. https://www.figma.com/deck/tFRGgSho2sEiq8mjW9pif8
  • Repository: https://github.com/Athar-HQ/Athar
  • Latest release: binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows. https://github.com/Athar-HQ/Athar/releases/latest

If you hunt infrastructure, send us your hunts as rules. You don’t have to write the YAML by hand: give your query and one host it found to an AI coding agent in the repository, and AGENTS.md tells it how to turn the query into a tested rule. And if something is missing, open an issue.

items.title: FIFA Alleged Breach – Hackers Claim Access to 12.2 GB of Sensitive Internal Documents
items.summary: FIFA has confirmed that hackers gained unauthorized access to a limited set of personal and business information. The Switzerland-based world football governing body has not confirmed a claim by the Handsome Boy Hacking Club (HBHC) that it obtained and published 12.2 GB of sensitive internal documents. The breach is confirmed, but the group has not verified the size or contents of the archive it claims to have released. A FIFA spokesperson told The Record on November 25 that the organization was working with relevant authorities, including law enforcement. FIFA condemned the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data. It did not answer the outlet’s follow-up questions about the incident. FIFA has not said how the hackers got in, when it detected the intrusion, or whose information was affected. In a November 21 post on X, Dark Web Informer said HBHC claimed to have taken files from FIFA’s Microsoft environment and internal governance systems. The group described the material as identity and immigration documents, information about executives, financial and legal records, and internal governance files and screenshots. Dark Web Informer said the claim was unverified. The group advertised the files for download and warned that some folders could contain corrupted or duplicate data. That makes the claimed archive size a poor measure of the breach’s impact. FIFA Alleged Breach A large archive can contain multiple copies of the same document, and its size does not show how many people were affected. The Record also reported that HBHC claimed it tried to extort FIFA before posting the files on a cybercrime forum. No public confirmation shows that FIFA’s files were encrypted. The group’s reference to a Microsoft environment does not identify a product or explain how the intruders got access. It does not establish that a Microsoft software flaw was involved or that any specific service, such as SharePoint, was breached. FIFA has not publicly named the affected systems. FIFA allegedly breached, 12.2 GB of sensitive internal documents leaked The Handsome Boy Hacking Club (HBHC) claims to have released data stolen from FIFA, the international governing body of football, headquartered in Switzerland. The group claims the files were extracted… pic.twitter.com/5X03OEZo2o — Dark Web Informer (@DarkWebInformer) November 21, 2026 If Microsoft cloud services were involved, audit logs could help investigators check for unusual sign-ins and see which files an account opened or downloaded. Cyber Security News previously covered the Microsoft cloud logging playbook , which explains how those records can help trace suspicious activity. The key question for affected people is whether their documents were among the files accessed or copied. In a November 23 statement, Spain’s LaLiga said an attacker stole personal data from a fan services platform between November 14 and 16. The platform served people registered with LaLiga and some clubs. The league said it blocked the attacker on November 16, notified Spain’s data protection agency and reported the incident to the National Police. It said the attack did not affect its other systems or disrupt the competition. No public evidence links the LaLiga incident to the FIFA breach. The two incidents involve different kinds of records. LaLiga identified a platform that held fan data. At the same time, FIFA has confirmed access to personal and business information without saying whose records were involved. Cyber Security News also previously reported on fake FIFA websites that collected personal information . That was a separate scam, not evidence that FIFA’s own systems had been breached. Anyone who receives an unexpected message asking them to upload identity documents in response to the breach should verify the request through an official channel before sharing anything. FIFA condemned the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data. It did not answer the outlet’s follow-up questions about the incident. FIFA has not said how the hackers got in, when it detected the intrusion, or whose information was affected.

In a November 21 post on X, Dark Web Informer said HBHC claimed to have taken files from FIFA’s Microsoft environment and internal governance systems.

The group described the material as identity and immigration documents, information about executives, financial and legal records, and internal governance files and screenshots. Dark Web Informer said the claim was unverified.

The group advertised the files for download and warned that some folders could contain corrupted or duplicate data. That makes the claimed archive size a poor measure of the breach’s impact.

FIFA Alleged Breach

A large archive can contain multiple copies of the same document, and its size does not show how many people were affected. The Record also reported that HBHC claimed it tried to extort FIFA before posting the files on a cybercrime forum. No public confirmation shows that FIFA’s files were encrypted.

The group’s reference to a Microsoft environment does not identify a product or explain how the intruders got access. It does not establish that a Microsoft software flaw was involved or that any specific service, such as SharePoint, was breached. FIFA has not publicly named the affected systems.

FIFA allegedly breached, 12.2 GB of sensitive internal documents leaked

The group claims the files were extracted… pic.twitter.com/5X03OEZo2o

— Dark Web Informer (@DarkWebInformer) November 21, 2026

If Microsoft cloud services were involved, audit logs could help investigators check for unusual sign-ins and see which files an account opened or downloaded.

Cyber Security News previously covered the Microsoft cloud logging playbook, which explains how those records can help trace suspicious activity. The key question for affected people is whether their documents were among the files accessed or copied.

In a November 23 statement, Spain’s LaLiga said an attacker stole personal data from a fan services platform between November 14 and 16. The platform served people registered with LaLiga and some clubs.

The two incidents involve different kinds of records. LaLiga identified a platform that held fan data. At the same time, FIFA has confirmed access to personal and business information without saying whose records were involved.

Cyber Security News also previously reported on fake FIFA websites that collected personal information. That was a separate scam, not evidence that FIFA’s own systems had been breached.

Anyone who receives an unexpected message asking them to upload identity documents in response to the breach should verify the request through an official channel before sharing anything.

The solutions below separate on where they center detection (user behavior, data movement, or analytics), whether they tell malice from carelessness, and how proportionately they can be run. items.title: Microsoft Warns State-Backed Hackers Are Using ARTEX AI Agents to Steal Credentials and Breach Networks
items.summary: State-backed hackers and financially motivated groups are using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework, to find exposed systems, steal credentials, and break into enterprise networks and cloud environments. In a November 25 report, Microsoft warned that the framework can move from scanning to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on the target’s defenses and how the operator uses it. The report does not describe a new exploit or a flaw in an AI model. Instead, ARTEX speeds up familiar techniques and reduces the need for an operator to intervene between steps. In one case, an AI agent went from searching public GitHub repositories for application secrets to extracting data from Azure Key Vault, Microsoft’s cloud service for storing secrets, in five minutes. Microsoft Threat Intelligence researchers identified six threat actors using ARTEX: Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon, and Salt Typhoon. Microsoft Warns State-Backed Hackers Are Using ARTEX AI Agents They describe ARTEX as a security testing framework abused by attackers, not a standalone malware family. As earlier coverage of internet-exposed AI hacking frameworks showed, these tools can support authorized security testing, but the same automation can also speed up intrusions. ARTEX divides work among several AI agents. A planner reviews what the framework has discovered, workers carry out assigned tasks, and a reporter documents confirmed findings. The framework updates a shared record of systems and findings as work progresses. That matters because an agent can act on a discovery while other tasks are still running, rather than waiting for a person to review the results. Microsoft’s ConnectWise supply chain investigation found that China-aligned Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate intrusions. The ConnectWise Microsoft 365 campaign involved stolen application credentials and sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 customer environments, not 2,250 confirmed breaches. ARTEX AI agent architecture (Source – Microsoft) The attackers relied on permissions customers had already granted to trusted applications. In multiple Storm-0940 intrusions, Microsoft observed the group reach privileged cloud access less than three hours after initial targeting. Microsoft recorded more than 151,000 failed sign-ins in one Storm-0940 campaign, with a peak of 2,900 failures per minute. Other activity was less obvious: ARTEX agents added credentials to applications to maintain access, and one application assigned itself the Global Administrator role. The previously reported ARTEX GitHub credential theft case illustrates a separate risk: a leaked application secret can expose cloud data without an employee account being compromised. How Defenders Can Detect and Contain ARTEX Activity Microsoft says the strongest signal is a sequence of events, not a single IP address or browser identifier. Look for bursts of web requests or failed sign-ins followed quickly by successful access, unusual server processes, or changes to cloud application permissions. A web server unexpectedly launching a command shell is worth investigating, especially if it coincides with new scripts in a web folder or rapid reads of files that hold credentials. For cloud investigations, collect application identity sign-in logs as well as employee sign-in logs. Microsoft Entra records those events separately. Teams should correlate them with audit logs for new application credentials and privileged role assignments. The FBI’s ARTEX security warning also underscores why defenders should check what an internet-facing service or trusted application can reach after it is compromised. Microsoft recommends patching exposed systems first, using web application firewalls in prevention mode after tuning, and rate-limiting bursts of requests. Enable secret scanning and push protection to catch credentials before they enter repositories. Revoke and replace exposed secrets, move workloads to managed identities where possible, and require phishing-resistant multifactor authentication for administrators. Microsoft also recommends enabling automatic attack disruption in Defender XDR to help contain compromised assets before attackers move to other systems. Correlate with bursts of probing. HTTP user agent norma Associated with requests from the framework’s built-in web-fetch tool. The value can change. Defender Antivirus detection Behavior:Win64/ArtexAI A behavioral detection for ARTEX-related components, not a file hash. Shared service webhook[.]site Observed in some ARTEX activity. State-backed hackers and financially motivated groups are using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework, to find exposed systems, steal credentials, and break into enterprise networks and cloud environments.

In a November 25 report, Microsoft warned that the framework can move from scanning to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on the target’s defenses and how the operator uses it.

The report does not describe a new exploit or a flaw in an AI model. Instead, ARTEX speeds up familiar techniques and reduces the need for an operator to intervene between steps.

In one case, an AI agent went from searching public GitHub repositories for application secrets to extracting data from Azure Key Vault, Microsoft’s cloud service for storing secrets, in five minutes.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence researchers identified six threat actors using ARTEX: Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon, and Salt Typhoon.

Microsoft Warns State-Backed Hackers Are Using ARTEX AI Agents

They describe ARTEX as a security testing framework abused by attackers, not a standalone malware family. As earlier coverage of internet-exposed AI hacking frameworks showed, these tools can support authorized security testing, but the same automation can also speed up intrusions.

ARTEX divides work among several AI agents. A planner reviews what the framework has discovered, workers carry out assigned tasks, and a reporter documents confirmed findings.

The framework updates a shared record of systems and findings as work progresses. That matters because an agent can act on a discovery while other tasks are still running, rather than waiting for a person to review the results.

Microsoft’s ConnectWise supply chain investigation found that China-aligned Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate intrusions.

The ConnectWise Microsoft 365 campaign involved stolen application credentials and sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 customer environments, not 2,250 confirmed breaches.

ARTEX AI agent architecture (Source – Microsoft)

The attackers relied on permissions customers had already granted to trusted applications. In multiple Storm-0940 intrusions, Microsoft observed the group reach privileged cloud access less than three hours after initial targeting.

Microsoft recorded more than 151,000 failed sign-ins in one Storm-0940 campaign, with a peak of 2,900 failures per minute. Other activity was less obvious: ARTEX agents added credentials to applications to maintain access, and one application assigned itself the Global Administrator role.

The previously reported ARTEX GitHub credential theft case illustrates a separate risk: a leaked application secret can expose cloud data without an employee account being compromised.

How Defenders Can Detect and Contain ARTEX Activity

Microsoft says the strongest signal is a sequence of events, not a single IP address or browser identifier. Look for bursts of web requests or failed sign-ins followed quickly by successful access, unusual server processes, or changes to cloud application permissions.

A web server unexpectedly launching a command shell is worth investigating, especially if it coincides with new scripts in a web folder or rapid reads of files that hold credentials.

For cloud investigations, collect application identity sign-in logs as well as employee sign-in logs. Microsoft Entra records those events separately.

Teams should correlate them with audit logs for new application credentials and privileged role assignments. The FBI’s ARTEX security warning also underscores why defenders should check what an internet-facing service or trusted application can reach after it is compromised.

Microsoft recommends patching exposed systems first, using web application firewalls in prevention mode after tuning, and rate-limiting bursts of requests. Enable secret scanning and push protection to catch credentials before they enter repositories.

Revoke and replace exposed secrets, move workloads to managed identities where possible, and require phishing-resistant multifactor authentication for administrators.

Microsoft also recommends enabling automatic attack disruption in Defender XDR to help contain compromised assets before attackers move to other systems.

The grammar-mistake era of phishing is over. AI now writes flawless lures, clones brands pixel-perfect, and personalizes at scale so anti-phishing has shifted from spotting typos to modeling behavior, verifying sender identity, and killing the malicious link or message after it lands.

The solutions below separate on detection depth against modern lures, impersonation and lookalike defense, and remediation speed. Proofpoint takes 1; Abnormal and Mimecast complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Proofpoint the threat-intel and impersonation-defense benchmark.

• Podium: Proofpoint, Abnormal Security (behavioral-AI catch), Mimecast (gateway-plus-awareness).

• Model split: intel-led gateways (Proofpoint, Mimecast, Microsoft) versus behavioral-AI layers (Abnormal, IRONSCALES) versus specialist link/isolation defense (Cloudflare Area 1, Vade, INKY).

• 2026 theme: AI-versus-AI the defining fight is machine-generated lures against machine-behavioral detection.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: phishing detection depth, impersonation/lookalike defense, behavioral/AI capability, remediation speed, user-reporting integration, and pricing clarity.

Weights: detection depth 25%, impersonation defense 25%, behavioral/AI 20%, remediation 15%, reporting integration 15%.

items.title: 4,000+ Servers Running AI Hacking Agents Are Exposed to the Internet and Actively Attacking
items.summary: The Shadowserver Foundation found around 4,200 internet-exposed instances of AI hacking frameworks on November 23, 2026, up from just under 3,700 a day earlier. Its November 25 report also documented more than 10,000 events from over 80 IP addresses identified as running these tools between November 9 and 23. The larger figure measures exposure. The smaller one counts sources that sent traffic to Shadowserver’s honeypots. The findings do not show that all 4,200 instances were attacking. Exposed AI Attack Framework instances per region – linear scale (source : Shadowserver) Shadowserver scans the internet daily for 15 AI attack frameworks and tracks exposure on its public dashboard. These tools use large language models to guide tasks such as finding exposed services and testing for known flaws with limited human input. 4,000+ Servers Expose AI Hacking Agents Security teams can use them for authorized testing. A public instance alone does not tell researchers who runs it or whether its activity is approved. Exposed AI Attack Framework instances per country (source : shadowserver ) ARTEX accounted for around 70% of exposed instances on most days. AntiFox, a version based on ARTEX, grew from a handful of instances to around 200. Together, they made up about three-quarters of observed instances on November 22. A jump in PentestCode deployments helped drive the next day’s increase. Nearly half of the exposed instances were in Asia, more than a third were in North America, and most of the rest were in Europe. Nearly nine in ten attacking IP addresses were fingerprinted as ARTEX Gateway (source : shadowserver ) The FBI’s November 13 advisory said some ARTEX-assisted intrusions moved from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. In a separate case, Cyber Security News reported on a CyberStrikeAI intrusion that exposed 3,392 user accounts. Those cases show what the tools can do in real intrusions. Shadowserver’s honeypot data measures attempted activity, not confirmed breaches. Honeypots are decoy systems that record suspicious traffic. Nearly nine in ten source IP addresses seen by Shadowserver were identified as running ARTEX Gateway. Half of the IP Addresses Tried to Relay Traffic (source : Shadowserver) A handful generated most of the events, and the busiest address was linked to PentAGI. Almost all sources were on cloud networks. Activity was concentrated in the United States and Hong Kong, but that likely reflects where the servers were hosted, not where the operators were based. About six in ten source addresses tried to relay traffic through the sensors. Direct requests often probed VPN gateways, web apps, and developer tools such as Jenkins. About one in ten source addresses sent exploit or injection attempts, most often targeting the Metabase flaw CVE-2023-38646 . Some also looked for .env files, which can contain database passwords and cloud API keys. The focus on known flaws echoes earlier reporting on ARTEX attacks . VPNs, Web Apps and Developer Tools were the Main Targets (source: Shadowserver) Shadowserver recommends checking its free Device Identification report for the ai-attack-framework label. If a deployment is approved, limit access to trusted addresses or a VPN, require strong authentication, and keep the software updated. If no one can verify that the deployment is approved, isolate it and investigate possible misuse. Most sources operated in short bursts, but a few sent traffic during every hour of the day over several days. Shadowserver advises teams to rate-limit repeated probes and make sure alerts are handled outside business hours. Mostly Short Bursts, But Some Ran Around The Clock (source: Shadowserver) Before blocking an address, check it against recent logs. Cloud IP addresses can be reassigned, and an old report may no longer describe the system using that address. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.title: Roundcube Webmail Flaws Could Let Hackers Execute Malicious Code and Expose Sensitive Data
items.summary: Roundcube released Webmail versions 1.6.22 and 1.7.7 on November 23, 2026, to address 12 security flaws. The updates fix weaknesses in how the browser-based email client handles attachments, displays messages, and connects to mail servers. The release notes describe flaws that could expose data and allow unauthorized email filter code to run . However, they do not confirm remote code execution on the webmail server or report active exploitation of these bugs. One fix stops Roundcube from passing unsafe PDF, PostScript, and SVG attachment content to ImageMagick, a tool used to process images. Roundcube had previously attempted to fix this issue. The project also revisited an HTTP request injection flaw in its ATD spellcheck backend, which could allow unintended requests. The release notes do not say which configurations are most at risk or whether either flaw could give an attacker control of the server. Several fixes address how Roundcube displays HTML email. Two flaws let message styling break out of the limits meant to keep it separate from the webmail interface. Another let SVG content load external resources despite the user’s remote-content settings, weakening a privacy control that helps prevent email tracking. Roundcube Webmail Flaws The update also closes a flaw that could expose responses handled by the CSS proxy. It fixes a gap in the HTML filter on systems running PHP versions earlier than 8.4. Two separate flaws could let unauthorized instructions enter Sieve scripts, which mail servers use to run rules such as sorting incoming messages. Another fix addresses XML injection in the XIMSS driver of Roundcube’s password plugin. The release also closes a denial-of-service flaw where the decoder for TNEF attachments, a format associated with Microsoft Outlook, could spend too long processing attachment data. The updates also stop Roundcube from falling back to unencrypted IMAP, SMTP, or ManageSieve connections when TLS encryption is configured. However, the mail server does not advertise the required capability. That matters because a setting that appears to require encryption did not always prevent an unencrypted connection. Administrators should back up their data and patch production systems promptly. The official Roundcube 1.6.22 release notes identify it as the final release in the 1.6 long-term support branch. Teams that cannot move to 1.7 immediately should apply 1.6.22 rather than wait for the migration. The Roundcube 1.7.7 release notes list the same security fixes, and Roundcube says only the 1.7 branch will receive future security updates. Cyber Security News previously covered CISA’s warning about exploited Roundcube vulnerabilities and a separate Roundcube flaw that let attackers track email opens . Those reports concern earlier bugs, not the flaws fixed in November. They offer two reasons to keep webmail current: attackers have targeted Roundcube before, and a flaw does not have to take over a server to compromise user privacy. For teams still on 1.6, this update closes the current gaps, but moving to 1.7 is what keeps future fixes available. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Details!

items.title: Critical SolarWinds Serv-U Flaws Could Let Hackers Gain Root Access and Take Control of Servers
items.summary: SolarWinds released Serv-U 2026.4 on November 24, 2026, fixing 18 vulnerabilities, including nine critical flaws, two of which could grant attackers root access on Linux servers, while the risk is lower on Windows. However, the same update also fixes a high-severity command injection flaw that affects only Windows installations. The Serv-U 2026.4 release notes identify CVE-2026-123172 and CVE-2026-123168 as the two flaws that could grant Linux root privileges. Both received severity scores of 9.1 out of 10. Root access goes beyond the control of the Serv-U application. It could let an attacker read or change protected files and alter settings on the host. Several other critical flaws let users with existing administrative access gain more power than their roles should allow. CVE-2026-82322 could let a domain group administrator become a Serv-U server administrator. Two separate flaws, CVE-2026-82320 and CVE-2026-82321, could let domain administrators gain system administrator rights. CVE-2026-123167 could let a domain administrator reach files that normally require higher privileges. These are not the only ways someone without an account could break in. Several instead increase the damage a compromised admin account could cause. Critical SolarWinds Serv-U Flaws Three more critical flaws affect how Serv-U checks file access. SolarWinds says CVE-2026-82315 and CVE-2026-82316 could let a domain administrator or someone with higher privileges access or modify protected files outside the intended directory, potentially allowing code execution. CVE-2026-82319 could let a similarly privileged user read and write application files. SolarWinds credited the Intigriti Bug Bounty Program for all nine critical reports. CVE Vulnerability Score / Severity CVE-2026-82322 Insecure direct object reference (IDOR) 9.1 / Critical CVE-2026-123172 Privilege escalation 9.1 / Critical CVE-2026-123167 Path traversal and privilege escalation 9.1 / Critical CVE-2026-123166 Command injection 7.2 / High CVE-2026-123165 HTTP response header injection 4.7 / Medium CVE-2026-123169 MFA code guessing and replay 5.4 / Medium CVE-2026-123170 Password brute force 6.5 / Medium CVE-2026-123171 Username enumeration 5.3 / Medium CVE-2026-82321 Type confusion and privilege escalation 9.1 / Critical CVE-2026-82320 Type confusion and privilege escalation 9.1 / Critical CVE-2026-82316 File access race condition 9.1 / Critical CVE-2026-82315 File access race condition 9.1 / Critical CVE-2026-82319 File access race condition and privilege escalation 9.1 / Critical CVE-2026-82317 Stored cross-site scripting (XSS) 6.8 / Medium CVE-2026-82313 Business logic flaw 8.4 / High CVE-2026-82314 Denial of service 4.9 / Medium CVE-2026-123168 Insufficient validation and privilege escalation 9.1 / Critical CVE-2026-123173 Out-of-bounds read in SSH key exchange 6.8 / High The update also fixes weak protections against repeated password and one-time code guesses, a flaw that exposes whether specific usernames exist, and a separate SSH flaw that could disclose data from server memory. The release notes do not report active exploitation of the newly disclosed flaws. Cyber Security News previously covered the Serv-U 2026.3 security fixes and CISA’s warning about a separate Serv-U flaw exploited in attacks . Administrators should prioritize upgrading to Serv-U 2026.4, starting with internet-facing Linux servers. Windows deployments also need the update because the lower risk from the critical flaws does not remove the Windows-only command injection risk. The Serv-U 2026.4 release includes OpenSSL 3.5 LTS and stops Serv-U from writing multi-factor authentication codes to its logs. Before installing the update, follow the SolarWinds Serv-U upgrade guide to back up the configuration and export the server identifier. If you are skipping more than one version, SolarWinds recommends checking its release notes aggregator for changes between releases. After updating, verify that the server reports version 2026.4 and test the sign-in and file transfer workflows your organization relies on. Security teams should also review recent administrator changes and unexpected file activity, since installing the update does not tell you whether a server was compromised before it was patched. The update also fixes weak protections against repeated password and one-time code guesses, a flaw that exposes whether specific usernames exist, and a separate SSH flaw that could disclose data from server memory.

The release notes do not report active exploitation of the newly disclosed flaws. Cyber Security News previously covered the Serv-U 2026.3 security fixes and CISA’s warning about a separate Serv-U flaw exploited in attacks.

Administrators should prioritize upgrading to Serv-U 2026.4, starting with internet-facing Linux servers. Windows deployments also need the update because the lower risk from the critical flaws does not remove the Windows-only command injection risk. The Serv-U 2026.4 release includes OpenSSL 3.5 LTS and stops Serv-U from writing multi-factor authentication codes to its logs.

Before installing the update, follow the SolarWinds Serv-U upgrade guide to back up the configuration and export the server identifier. If you are skipping more than one version, SolarWinds recommends checking its release notes aggregator for changes between releases.

After updating, verify that the server reports version 2026.4 and test the sign-in and file transfer workflows your organization relies on.

Security teams should also review recent administrator changes and unexpected file activity, since installing the update does not tell you whether a server was compromised before it was patched.

items.title: What Two Million Canary Prompts Reveal About AI Supply Chain Security
items.summary: Executive Summary To evaluate the security of the AI supply chain, Dragos seeded approximately two million AI prompts with canary URLs and credentials. The investigation revealed that prompt data was stolen from at least three AI hosting providers and from the system of a Chinese AI lab, which accessed secret URLs from prompts marked for zero data retention. No security team can audit the providers its prompts pass through, whether they are foreign or domestic. Every team can test its own side: the models it calls and what goes into each prompt. Qualys TotalAI maps the models and AI services in use, red-teams any model with a chat completion endpoint (including foreign models), and detects secrets before they reach a prompt. Inside the Canary Experiment In a study published on November 19, 2026 , a team from Dragos, led by Chief Research Officer HD Moore, sent approximately two million prompts to popular AI services from July through November, tracing around 2,000 request routes. Each prompt carried canary tokens: unique URLs and live AWS keys linked to empty accounts that were fully monitored. If a URL was accessed, it indicated that the system had read the prompt; if a key was used, it showed that someone had stolen a credential. What the Dragos Canary Study Exposed Breached Providers Attackers have stolen prompt data from at least three AI hosting providers, and Dragos reports that these providers were unaware of the breaches until they were notified. In the largest breach, every canary request Dragos sent during several late-October windows was stolen. This included requests that the provider had rejected before any models had a chance to run. Attackers tested the AWS keys, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, attempted to enable Amazon Bedrock models, create Bedrock API keys, and add IAM users. One adversary later used ARTEX, an LLM-driven penetration testing framework, to confirm that the keys were active. Leaky Routes AI routers forward requests to pools of hosting providers, and every hop can access the full prompt. A Zero Data Retention (ZDR) setting is intended to ensure that the service an application calls does not retain prompts or responses, yet Dragos found ZDR-marked requests stolen or scraped further down the route. They also discovered instances of marketplace sellers logging prompts and a router quietly forwarding some traffic to these marketplaces. A Foreign Lab Reading Flagged Prompts A Chinese AI lab’s systems fetched secret URLs from more than half of the prompts sent to its models, including about two-thirds of those marked ZDR; U.S. resellers of its models triggered the same scraper. In a later statement, the lab said an internal security monitoring process extracted and probed the URLs, and that it has disabled that process for forwarded API traffic. Providers Cannot Be Audited. The Customer Side Can Be Tested. Every finding turned on one fact: whatever sits in a prompt, from a live credential to customer data or source code, can be seen by every hop on the route. A credential turns that exposure into an intrusion. No model test can show what a provider’s infrastructure does with a request. Security teams can only test their own systems, and Qualys TotalAI answers four questions about this. 1. Which Models and Routes Are in Use? Qualys TotalAI leverages existing Qualys sensors. Cloud Agents and scanners can fingerprint AI software and GPUs, cloud connectors map managed AI services, Container Security covers AI workloads, and a browser plug-in shows workforce AI usage. Qualys Container Runtime Security adds evidence about where containerized AI applications connect. Security teams can correlate DNS and outbound TCP events from monitored workloads to track direct connections to AI routers or provider endpoints outside their approved list. For requests routed through a provider, they can use router or gateway records to identify the reported inference provider. Qualys TotalAI enhances this visibility by testing supported model endpoints for sensitive information disclosures. Self-hosting, which Dragos recommends where affordable, takes third parties off the route but makes the model server the target. Qualys detects known vulnerabilities and default credentials in servers such as Ollama, vLLM and LiteLLM, and AI detection and response (AI-DR)¹, an extension of Qualys EDR to AI assets, is designed to catch attacks on that infrastructure as they happen. 2. Do The AI Models In Use Leak Their Context? Red-team tests show what a model gives away under attack. TotalAI evaluates any model with a chat completion endpoint , including foreign models, against 300+ attack scenarios mapped to OWASP , MITRE ATLAS , and the EU AI Act, including 21 sensitive information disclosure checks. A model that discloses a real credential from its system prompt, retrieved documents or tool output proves it sat in the model’s context, where every hop could see it. When a test fails, automated guardrail remediation¹ is designed to push the fix into Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. 3. Can a Secret Reach the Prompt? Guardrails control what a model repeats, not what it was sent: in the largest breach, attackers stole some requests rejected before any model ran. The test that matters is whether a secret can reach the prompt at all, and that starts where secrets live. Qualys scanning detects exposed secrets in container images, CI/CD pipelines, and code repositories. This leak class was responsible for a provider notice in November, where an AI coding agent committed a credential to a public repository. TotalAI MCP scans test the servers that agents source context from for credential exposure. Additionally, MCP tool-call tracing¹ is designed to show what each tool call passes into an agent’s context. Secrets also enter at run time, pasted by users or returned by tools, where static scans cannot see them. Policy-based runtime controls with inline blocking¹ are designed to block or redact secrets before a request exits the organization. A key that never reaches the first hop cannot be stolen further down the route. 4. What Can a Stolen Key Reach? Qualys analysis of a 2026 intrusion traced an exposed AWS key to a complete cloud takeover in under ten minutes. TotalCloud CIEM shows what each cloud identity can access and flags excess privileges. Its posture checks cover AI services such as Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker, and Azure OpenAI. TruRisk Insights AI attack paths¹ are designed to connect exposed endpoints, excess permissions, and sensitive data into one prioritized path. What to Do This Week Map the models and routes in use. Flag any connection to a router or provider that no one approved, as well as any self-hosted model server that can be reached without authentication. Test the models in use, including foreign ones, after every change to a model or prompt. Find secrets in code, images, and agent context. Remove them before an agent can load them. Rotate secrets in prompts covered by any provider or router notice, and give agents short-lived, least-privilege keys. Hunt for the indicators. Search CloudTrail for ARTEX user agents artex-agent and artex-judge-r121 , Bedrock enablement, new Bedrock API keys, and new IAM users. Dragos also recommends pinning providers and verifying Zero Data Retention on every hop. Test the Models No One Can Audit The Dragos study found no new class of vulnerability: exposed credentials and broken privacy promises, moving through a supply chain customers can barely see. No team can audit the provider side. Every team can test the models it calls and keep secrets out of the prompt. Learn how to map your AI in use, test its models, and catch secrets before they reach a prompt. Start Your 30-Day Free Trial Organizations already running Qualys Cloud Agents have a first AI inventory waiting, with no separate AI security agent to deploy. Key Takeaways Treat any secret that has appeared in a prompt as exposed. A privacy flag is a promise from one hop, but a prompt crosses several. Providers cannot be audited from outside, but models can be tested and the first hop mapped. Test whether a secret can reach the prompt. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What did the Dragos canary study find? From July through November 2026, Dragos sent about two million prompts carrying canary URLs and AWS keys to AI services. It found prompt data stolen from at least three AI hosting providers, marketplace sellers logging prompts, and a Chinese AI lab’s systems fetching secret URLs from prompts marked for zero data retention. Can security teams test AI models they do not host? Yes, for model behavior: TotalAI tests any model with a chat completion endpoint, including foreign models. What a provider’s infrastructure does with a request is outside what any model test can see. Does Zero Data Retention protect AI prompts? Zero Data Retention (ZDR) protects a prompt only at the hop that honors it. In the Dragos study, ZDR-flagged requests were stolen inside breached providers, and their secret URLs fetched downstream. Security teams should verify the route as well as the settings, including what each hop’s retention terms exempt from. What is AI supply chain security? AI supply chain security means controlling every service that handles an organization’s AI traffic: models, routers, inference providers, and the agents that build each prompt. How should organizations secure self-hosted AI models? Treat model servers such as Ollama, vLLM and LiteLLM like any other exposed service: patch known vulnerabilities, remove default credentials and require authentication on every API. Qualys publishes detections for specific issues with Ollama, vLLM, and LiteLLM. ¹ Features expected to be available by the end of Q4 2026. Product features, functionality, and release dates may change at any time at Qualys’s sole discretion.

items.title: Make post-quantum cryptography updates routine with AWS-LC
items.summary: As your organization plans upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), you should also think about cryptographic agility to more easily update algorithms used to protect your data. Changes to cryptography and related protocols aren’t new, but PQC is accelerating the pace at which organizations must add new algorithms and remove old ones to keep up with changing regulations and evolving business risk. AWS believes our key to success is standardizing on one cryptographic library that embodies three key properties: compatibility, assurance, and performance. In this blog post, you’ll learn how we think of the cost and friction of ongoing cryptographic updates in terms of these properties. You’ll learn how AWS built AWS-LC to embody these properties, thus making cryptographic upgrades straightforward and low-impact for ourselves and our customers. For custom applications where you can’t yet use AWS services and must operate your own stacks, this post also shares why you might consider using AWS-LC as your standardized library. Every cryptographic algorithm used to protect your data today has an expiration date, even if no regulator has set one yet. Algorithms that were once the standard, such as MD5 and SHA-1, have been retired. Standards are revised and flaws are found in implementations. The move to post-quantum cryptography is the current wave of changes, with dates set by governments and regulators to complete the transition. PQC itself will progress in phases to enable hybrid and pure post-quantum algorithms and then deprecate traditional cryptography. Each change reaches your systems as a software library update, so the practical question is how often you can roll out a new version of your cryptographic library, and what each rollout costs. At AWS, we think of this cost in terms of three properties. Compatibility means an update doesn’t require application changes. Assurance means new code can be trusted when it ships, without a long bake period. Performance means a new algorithm doesn’t add so much computational overhead or latency that it gives teams a reason to wait. This post describes how AWS-LC provides each property, and how you can apply the same approach to the cryptography you own. AWS-LC is the general-purpose cryptographic library that AWS maintains and uses across its services. It is derived from BoringSSL, which originated from OpenSSL. If you’ve called an AWS API, AWS-LC was used on the server side. Through s2n-tls, it provides hybrid post-quantum key exchange on AWS service endpoints and in services like Application Load Balancer and Network Load Balancer . It’s also the cryptography under aws-lc-rs for Rust, the default provider for rustls , and under the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider for Java. Because so much of AWS depends on one library, we built it to be updated often. AWS-LC keeps an OpenSSL-compatible API so applications can replace algorithms without a rewrite. It uses formal verification to prove selected algorithm implementations correct. It optimizes algorithm implementations to reduce the latency and compute costs that new algorithms add. The same properties work outside AWS. For example, 1Password used AWS-LC to move its clients to hybrid post-quantum key exchange with no application code changes. Hand off what you can, standardize what you keep Each piece of cryptography you own is one more thing to change at every transition. By owning as little of your cryptographic stack as your constraints or requirements allow, and using AWS services to manage the rest, you can minimize your ongoing responsibility and operational risk. If your workload relies solely on managed services like AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) and managed resources like Elastic Load Balancer or Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) , you’re already reaping the benefits of AWS-LC and the AWS shared responsibility model. You only need to keep your clients and resource configurations updated. Many organizations can rely on AWS to provide the infrastructure and basic automation, but still own and manage the endpoints and applications where most of the work happens. For these components, it’s helpful to standardize on as few cryptographic libraries as possible. With fewer libraries, your team learns each one well: how to configure it, run it, and update it. The library you standardize on also decides how often you can update it. If an update requires application changes, ships new code that no one trusts yet, or adds compute and latency, teams have a reason to wait. This post describes how AWS-LC provides each property, and how you can apply the same approach to the cryptography you own.

AWS-LC is the general-purpose cryptographic library that AWS maintains and uses across its services. It is derived from BoringSSL, which originated from OpenSSL. The same properties work outside AWS. For example, 1Password used AWS-LC to move its clients to hybrid post-quantum key exchange with no application code changes.
